articles.title: Talking Point: NVIDIA’s JUPITER breakthrough brings practical quantum computing a step closer - Intelligent CIO
articles.summary: Talking Point: NVIDIA’s JUPITER breakthrough brings practical quantum computing a step closer  Intelligent CIO
articles.full_text:
Quantum computing is entering an exciting new phase as researchers make measurable progress towards overcoming challenges that have constrained its potential in medicine, finance and materials science.
NVIDIA’s latest experiment at Germany’s Jülich Supercomputing Centre suggests practical quantum computing is becoming more achievable.
Using JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer, NVIDIA researchers simulated a 104-qubit fault-tolerant quantum processor under realistic noise conditions. NVIDIA calls it the largest comprehensive simulation of its kind. The work also tested ‘magic-state cultivation’, a technique designed to significantly reduce the hardware requirements associated with correcting quantum errors.
NVIDIA says the approach requires 90% fewer physical qubits than previous methods. If these efficiency gains can be reproduced in physical quantum systems, they could advance commercially viable quantum computing.
Quantum error correction remains one of the industry’s most demanding technical challenges. Qubits are sensitive to environmental disturbances, making reliable calculations difficult. Fault tolerance addresses this problem by introducing resources that protect quantum information and enable dependable operations.
Reducing those requirements could improve the economics of quantum computing. Smaller systems, lower costs and more efficient architectures would make the technology increasingly accessible to researchers, businesses and industrial users.
The experiment shows how simulation can accelerate progress before hardware is constructed.
NVIDIA initially developed and tested its simulation techniques on GB200 infrastructure before scaling them to 8,192 GPUs on JUPITER. Its cuQuantum software and CUDA-Q platform supported the calculations. According to the company, development work helped reduce simulation times from weeks to days.
This acceleration matters because quantum computing development depends on testing complex architectures, identifying potential failures and refining designs. The ability to conduct these experiments more efficiently could shorten development cycles and help researchers concentrate resources on the most promising approaches.
It also highlights a productive relationship between classical and quantum computing.
Rather than competing technologies, high-performance computing and quantum systems are becoming complementary components of future computational infrastructure. Classical supercomputers can support quantum processor design, error correction research and the eventual operation of sophisticated quantum machines.
Europe has reason to welcome the breakthrough. JUPITER demonstrates the strategic value of investing in public research infrastructure. By providing the computational capacity required for pioneering quantum research, the Jülich Supercomputing Centre is strengthening Europe’s position within a competitive international technology landscape.
This illustrates how European infrastructure and American technology expertise can combine to advance scientific discovery.
Challenges remain. Researchers must validate simulation results experimentally and demonstrate that theoretical efficiency gains translate into reliable hardware operating at commercially meaningful scale.
The direction of progress is encouraging. The significance of NVIDIA’s achievement lies not simply in the number of simulated qubits but in its contribution to solving the practical problems that have delayed quantum computing’s development.
By reducing resource requirements, accelerating research and improving the understanding of fault-tolerant architectures, advances such as this could help transform quantum computing from an emerging scientific capability into a powerful industrial technology.
JUPITER has demonstrated that the journey towards useful quantum computing is gaining momentum. The next challenge is translating that momentum into working machines.

articles.title: Ukraine learns to fight without Starlink as Musk plays politics with satellites
articles.summary: Ukraine has changed drone and war-fighting tech to reduce reliance on Starlink.
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it.
As the world’s largest communications satellite network, Starlink can typically support high-speed Internet and data streams for any user or vehicle equipped with a relatively compact Starlink terminal. This has enabled Ukraine to maintain vital communications for both civilian purposes and military operations—and has also expanded the Ukrainian military’s capability to remotely control or provide guidance to drones used in both air defense against Russian attacks and for striking back at Russian targets.
“Starlink currently offers some of the best satellite coverage available, with virtually no competitors when you consider the combination of cost, availability, and ease of use,” according to the head of hardware R&D at the Ukrainian defense company BlueBird Tech, who provided comments to Ars anonymously for security reasons. “In practical terms, the main limitation is the need to position the antenna so it can receive signals from the satellites.”Read full article

articles.title: Ep. 040 - ASML Is Building a Hybrid Bonding Tool, and We Have the Patents (AI Supply Chain)｜SemiAnalysis - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: Ep. 040 - ASML Is Building a Hybrid Bonding Tool, and We Have the Patents (AI Supply Chain)｜SemiAnalysis  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
ASML's patented carousel-style hybrid bonding tool, analyzed via patents, targets logic die-to-wafer bonding while HBM adoption is judged unlikely before 2029, as China pursues hybrid bonding to offset lithography limits.
Summary
ASML is developing a hybrid bonding tool that inverts the standard pick-and-place architecture, moving the wafer to the die on a conveyor track rather than the die to the wafer, according to SemiAnalysis's Howie and Sherry Zhang, who say patent filings reveal the design. The episode spends most of its 34 minutes on the technical and economic case for hybrid bonding — why it matters for logic and not yet for HBM, what alignment and cleanliness demand of any tool, and how China is using it as a substitute for lithography scaling — with the ASML patent itself as the entry point rather than the whole conversation.
Howie and Sherry Zhang are SemiAnalysis analysts who co-wrote the underlying research with host Jordan Nanos, and they bring a teardown of a Huawei phone to the discussion as a physical example of hybrid bonding in production silicon. The reader should walk away with a clear picture of the competitive map in hybrid bonding tools (BESI, ASMPT, EVG versus a front-end entrant), the reasons the analysts push HBM adoption out to 2029 or later, and the parallel supply-chain shift toward 6x12 photomasks for High-NA EUV.
ASML's patent inverts the tool: the wafer travels to the die
The core finding is architectural. In a conventional die-to-wafer tool from BESI or ASMPT, a static base wafer sits in place and a pick-and-place head lifts each chiplet, aligns it, and sets it down on the bond pads; the die moves and the tool stays still. ASML's patented design puts each die on a carrier that rides a conveyor track — supplied by SuperTrak Conveyance, a startup the analysts researched — past a series of stations for measurement and plasma activation, ending at a bonding station where the wafer rises to meet the die.
The analysts trace the idea to a tip-off from a Twitter account they call "Litos, Lithos Crafty," who posted a series of tweets spotting the pattern. From there the team researched SuperTrak and compared the design against incumbent tools. Sherry Zhang stresses the tool is several years out: "It's several years out, but it's at least worth discussing because it's very different to all the current tools out there."
The strategic logic is that ASML comes from front-end lithography, where sub-nanometer overlay control is routine — "easily order of magnitude higher precision" than pick-and-place, per Howie. As hybrid bonding pitches tighten and the number of signals per square millimeter between two dies becomes the binding constraint, overlay stops being ASML's problem. Its problem becomes mechanical: every station, including the final bonding step, must physically descend to a die that never leaves the track.
flowchart TD
    A["Die placed on carrier"] --> B["Carrier enters conveyor track"]
    B --> C["Metrology station measures die orientation"]
    C --> D["Plasma activation station"]
    D --> E["Bonding station: wafer rises to meet die"]
    E --> F["Annealing and downstream processing"]
That inversion creates two open engineering questions the analysts flag. First, maintaining measurement accuracy when the metrology apparatus itself moves to approach the die. Second, cleanliness across a track spanning several meters and square meters of exposed area — far below front-end transistor cleanroom standards, but still enough that a single particle ruins a bond. Howie also notes the non-standard form factor likely forces co-design agreements with companies that supply pre-bonding process steps, unless ASML builds those functions itself.
Hybrid bonding is a logic play; HBM adoption slips to 2029 or later
The analysts restate a claim from their February 2024 article: HBM will not adopt die-to-wafer hybrid bonding before 2029, if at all. The reasoning is economic, not technical. For logic, hybrid bonding lets designers split functional units across two layers so signal wires between them run a much shorter distance and in far greater number than a side-by-side layout allows. Howie holds up a Huawei XT2 phone containing the 9050 chip — which he describes as the first mobile phone chip to use hybrid bonding across two separate wafers — as the proof case, citing a clock speed of up to 2.7 GHz without raising voltage or power.
For memory, the benefit is different: more gigabytes per HBM stack within silicon's roughly 775-micron thickness ceiling. Howie puts the best case at about 50% higher capacity per stack. Against that, hybrid bonding is far more expensive than the reflow or thermo-compression bonding (TCB) memory makers use today, and the demand signal has moved the other way — AI labs and other customers have reportedly asked memory vendors to reduce layer counts for a given performance and bandwidth. "If you don't have to use hybrid bonding, then you shouldn't," Howie says.
Sherry Zhang adds that die-to-wafer is harder than wafer-to-wafer on both alignment accuracy and throughput, and that mature tools meeting both requirements are scarce. She points listeners to a separate SemiAnalysis writeup on HBM economics (referenced as covering "D SVEC" and stacking economics) for the full cost case.
The analysts are openly skeptical of vendor roadmaps here. They note ASML's 2024 roadmap shows hybrid bonding across NAND and DRAM, and compare it to ASML's earlier transistor-density projections of 300–500 million transistors per square millimeter that reality never approached. "Do take those with a grain of salt," Howie says.
| Segment | Primary motive | Status per the analysts | 
|---|---|---|
| Logic (mobile, data center) | Shorter inter-layer wiring, IP partitioning, power efficiency | In production (Huawei 9050); AMD SoIC and 3D V-Cache cited as earlier examples | 
| HBM / DRAM | Higher gigabytes per stack within thickness limit | Not before 2029, if at all — ROI fails versus TCB | 
| NAND / DRAM (ASML roadmap) | Vendor roadmap claim | Skeptical; roadmap optimism serves tool sales | 
Alignment and cleanliness decide yield, which is why front-end vendors are entering
Two requirements govern whether any hybrid bonding tool works, and the analysts treat them as the lens for judging ASML's design. Alignment means measuring where bond pads actually sit relative to expectation and compensating across six degrees of freedom — X, Y, rotation, and out-of-plane tilt — as the wafer approaches the die. Cleanliness means guaranteeing a particle-free surface from the moment a die is cleaned at one station to the moment it reaches bonding.
The cleanliness stakes are severe because of how the bond forms: dielectric-to-dielectric oxide bonding first, then annealing, during which the copper expands to fill the remaining gap. A trapped particle lifts the silicon around it, so the defect spreads well beyond the particle's footprint. Howie likens it to a wedge that prevents the whole surface from bonding. Sherry Zhang ties both requirements directly to yield and throughput, and argues they are why hybrid bonding now resembles a front-end process — and why front-end toolmakers beyond ASML are moving in.
China is using hybrid bonding as a substitute for lithography scaling
For Chinese chipmakers facing process-technology limits, hybrid bonding is a way to keep improving performance per watt without EUV. Howie's framing is blunt: with more silicon area available at a given power envelope, you can run at lower voltage, cut leakage, and gain efficiency. Hybrid bonding is a better version of simply making the die bigger, because the two layers sit directly atop each other with dense wiring between them.
The Huawei example shows the mechanism. Latency-critical functional units move closer together on the top layer while non-critical structures such as SRAM move to the bottom layer, out of the way. Howie says Huawei's roadmaps target full "logic folding" — hybrid bonded data center accelerators — by 2030, at bond pitches far tighter than TSMC's SoIC, and eventually three layers, which he notes would cut yield further and therefore multiply tool demand for the same output.
Sherry Zhang says Chinese toolmakers including NAURA and AMEC have made moves — acquisitions or investments — to build hybrid bonding and advanced packaging capability. On export controls, she declines to predict policy but says the domestic supply-chain effort has shifted from state-led to coordinated directly among toolmakers and fabs, designing to China's specific constraints. "If there are export controls... the export controls could accelerate or push them," she says, pointing to the rising localization rate of recent years.
Howie extends the split to design tools: Western EDA has never needed to partition individual core components like multipliers, timing relays, and buffers across two layers, while Huawei has teamed with design companies to build that flow. AMD's SoIC partitioning, by contrast, is simpler — CPU logic on one layer, L3 cache and SRAM on another, with a clean dividing line.
The 6x12 photomask is High-NA's fix for half-size reticles, and it reshapes the mask supply chain
High-NA EUV's anamorphic optics squeeze the mask pattern 8x in one dimension and only 4x in the other, halving maximum die size to roughly 400 square millimeters versus today's 850. The interim fix is design-side stitching — imec and ASML have both discussed dedicating specific floor-plan regions to stitching, sometimes using non-High-NA layers. The durable fix, targeted for the 2030 timeframe, is a 6x12 mask that doubles the mask length in one dimension and restores full-reticle exposure.

articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Diffusion Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor diffusion equipment market is entering a structurally significant phase as chipmakers ramp investments in leading-edge logic and memory capacity. Diffusion equipment, which includes batch furnaces and related systems for dopant introduction and thermal processing, sits on the critical path of every wafer fab. Demand is being pulled forward by the transition to sub-3nm gate-all-around logic and 200-plus-layer 3D NAND, where precise thermal budgets and contamination control become non-negotiable.
At the same time, national semiconductor self-sufficiency programs across the US, Europe, Japan, and India are creating new fab clusters, each requiring localized qualification and support infrastructure. The supply landscape remains concentrated among a handful of global OEMs, protected by deep process integration IP and high switching costs. Pricing power is shifting toward service and upgrades, with recurring revenue streams often exceeding initial tool cost.
This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, end-use sectors, regional dynamics, competitive positioning, and the qualification burden that shapes supplier selection. It is designed for equipment manufacturers, subsystem suppliers, investors, and strategic entrants seeking a clear view of where value pools are forming and how procurement logic is evolving.
The baseline scenario for the global semiconductor diffusion equipment market points to steady expansion through 2035, supported by the inexorable push toward advanced process nodes and the geographic diversification of fab capacity. The market is expected to register a CAGR of approximately 6.5% over the forecast period, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to around 185 by 2035. This growth is not linear; it will be punctuated by capex cycles tied to leading-edge foundry and memory investments, but the underlying trajectory remains positive.
The strongest demand pull comes from the transition to gate-all-around logic at 3nm and below, and from 3D NAND stacks exceeding 200 layers, both of which require tighter thermal budget control and higher equipment performance. Diffusion equipment demand is also being supported by the build-out of new fabs in the United States, Europe, Japan, and India, driven by government incentives. However, these new facilities will require extensive qualification cycles, delaying revenue recognition. The aftermarket for refurbished and legacy-node equipment provides a stable counter-cyclical buffer, particularly for automotive and industrial semiconductors.
Supply remains concentrated, with fewer than ten global players controlling the majority of system-level design-ins. Pricing power is concentrated in the service and upgrade layer, where proprietary consumables and process know-how create recurring revenue. Risks include geopolitical export controls, which could fragment the market further, and the potential for a capex digestion phase after the current investment wave. Overall, the outlook is cautiously optimistic, with growth driven by technology transitions and geographic expansion rather than unit-volume increases alone.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Transition to advanced nodes (sub-3nm gate-all-around logic and 200+ layer 3D NAND) requiring tighter thermal budget control and higher equipment performance
- Geographic diversification of semiconductor manufacturing driven by national self-sufficiency policies, creating new fab clusters and parallel qualification pathways
- Rising demand for mature-node semiconductors in automotive, industrial, and IoT applications, sustaining demand for refurbished and legacy diffusion equipment
- Increasing complexity of device architectures, including 3D structures and new materials, which raises the number of diffusion steps per wafer
- Growth in memory capacity investments, particularly DRAM and 3D NAND, as data center and AI workloads drive bit demand
- Government incentives and subsidies for domestic semiconductor production in the US, EU, Japan, and India, accelerating fab construction and equipment orders
Potential Growth Constraints
- High qualification burden and long design-in cycles for new equipment, which slow supplier diversification and delay revenue from new fabs
- Geopolitical export controls and trade restrictions that fragment the market and limit access to certain regions and customers
- Cyclicality of semiconductor capex, with potential digestion phases after periods of heavy investment leading to temporary demand declines
- Technical complexity and high R&D costs required to keep pace with advanced node requirements, posing barriers for smaller suppliers
- Supply chain constraints for critical components such as high-purity quartz and specialty ceramics, which can extend lead times and increase costs

Semiconductor Foundry (estimated share: 45%)
The foundry segment represents the largest and most technologically demanding end-use sector for semiconductor diffusion equipment. Foundries are ramping production at 5nm, 3nm, and below, where gate-all-around transistor architectures require precise dopant placement and ultra-low contamination levels. Diffusion furnaces are used for well formation, source/drain doping, and thermal annealing steps, with each advanced node adding process steps and tighter specifications. The demand story here is driven by capacity expansions at leading foundries such as TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and Intel Foundry, as well as the emergence of new foundries in the US, Europe, and Japan.
Key demand-side indicators include wafer starts per month at advanced nodes, capital expenditure guidance from major foundries, and the number of new fab projects announced. As foundries transition to gate-all-around and eventually complementary FET architectures, the requirement for diffusion equipment with higher temperature uniformity, faster ramp rates, and reduced particle contamination will intensify. This segment is expected to grow at a CAGR above the market average, supported by the relentless pursuit of Moore's Law and the increasing complexity of logic chips for AI, mobile, and high-performance computing applications. Memory manufacturers are a critical demand driver for diffusion equipment, particularly as 3D NAND stacks exceed 200 layers and DRAM scaling continues below 1-alpha nodes. In 3D NAND, diffusion processes are essential for creating the alternating dielectric layers and for doping the polysilicon channel, with each additional layer increasing the number of thermal steps and the need for high-throughput batch furnaces. DRAM scaling, meanwhile, requires precise dopant control for buried wordlines and capacitor structures. The demand story is supported by the growing bit demand from data centers, AI accelerators, and consumer devices, which is pushing memory makers to invest in new capacity and technology upgrades.
Key indicators include memory capex plans from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, as well as wafer capacity additions for 3D NAND and DRAM. The transition to 3D NAND with string stacking and CMOS-under-array architectures will require new diffusion processes and equipment upgrades. This segment is expected to grow in line with the overall market, with cyclicality tied to memory pricing and inventory cycles. articles.summary: TSMC explores rare-earth-free equipment to counter China controls  electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) is exploring alternatives to rare-earth components in its factory equipment. This move aims to mitigate risks from China's export controls on rare-earth materials, which could disrupt advanced chip production.
Highlights
- TSMC is exploring alternatives to rare-earth components in its factory equipment.
- The move aims to reduce risks from China's export controls on rare-earth materials.
- Rare-earth magnets are crucial for motors in highly automated chip production factories.
- US and Taiwan are also cooperating to diversify critical-mineral supply chains.
China last year placed certain rare-earth materials, magnets, and related processing technology under export controls, requiring licences. Rare-earth magnets are commonly used in motors for industrial equipment, including machinery in highly automated factories like those operated by TSMC.
A shortage of these specialised parts could disrupt chip production for customers in smartphone, AI system, data centre, and defence supply chains. TSMC has surveyed suppliers about using rare-earth-free motors in factory-automation equipment, three industry executives briefed by the company stated.
TSMC's efforts align with statements from the United States and Taiwan about reducing reliance on Chinese rare-earth and critical-mineral supply chains. Raymond F. Greene, director of the American Institute in Taiwan, said in June that the United States is collaborating with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative supply sources and enhance processing capacity.
Taiwan's Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin stated in February that the government would support the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) in developing rare-earth technologies. Plans include establishing a pilot production line within three years, aiming to meet an estimated 50 per cent of Taiwan's domestic demand.
US officials have engaged ITRI in discussions about diversifying critical-mineral supply chains, according to a person at a US-based think tank. ITRI confirmed it is working with Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs on a rare-earth project.

articles.title: Micron vs. Texas Instruments: Which Semiconductor Stock Has the Edge? - The Globe and Mail

articles.full_text:
Micron Technology, Inc.MU and Texas Instruments IncorporatedTXN are two major U.S. semiconductor manufacturers benefiting from rising chip demand, but their growth drivers differ.
Micron specializes in DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers, while Texas Instruments supplies analog and embedded processing chips for industrial, automotive and other markets. With Micron riding an AI-driven memory boom and Texas Instruments benefiting from a recovery in chip demand, which stock offers the better investment opportunity?
Their latest quarterly results, growth prospects and valuations provide important clues. Let’s delve deeper.
MU: AI Memory Demand Creates Growth Opportunity
Micron delivered exceptional fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results, with revenues surging to $54.23 billion from $11.32 billion a year-ago quarter. Fourth-quarter non-GAAP earnings of $33.42 per share jumped more than 11-fold from $3.03 in the year-ago quarter. Full-fiscal 2026 revenues reached $133.19 billion, more than tripling from fiscal 2025, while data center revenues quadrupled. Fiscal 2026 non-GAAP earnings increased to $75.52 per share from $8.29 in fiscal 2025, and management expects fiscal 2027 to be even stronger.
Micron Technology, Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Micron Technology, Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Micron Technology, Inc. Quote
AI infrastructure expansion is a major growth driver. Demand for HBM, server DRAM and data center SSDs is increasing as AI models require greater memory capacity and faster data access. Micron's fourth-quarter data center SSD revenues approached $10 billion, more than 10 times the year-ago level. It has also secured agreements covering most of its calendar year 2027 HBM supply, with higher prices expected to improve profitability.
Long-term strategic customer agreements offer another advantage. Micron reported 26 such agreements, representing an estimated more than 35% of revenues through 2030, alongside $32 billion in customer financial commitments. Its first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue guidance of $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion, signals continued momentum.
However, Micron remains exposed to memory-price swings, supply-demand changes and heavy manufacturing investment. Its expansion plans also require time and capital before new facilities contribute meaningfully. Any slowdown in AI spending or easing of memory shortages could pressure earnings.
TXN: Broad-Based Recovery Supports Steady Growth
Texas Instruments reported third-quarter 2026 revenues of $6.06 billion, up 28% year over year and 10.8% sequentially. Net income increased 78% to $2.43 billion, while earnings per share rose 77% to $2.62. Both analog and embedded processing businesses recorded year-over-year growth, reflecting improving demand across major end markets.
Texas Instruments Incorporated Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Texas Instruments Incorporated price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Texas Instruments Incorporated Quote
Industrial revenues increased more than 40% year over year, automotive revenues grew in the mid-teens, and data center revenues climbed approximately 95%. This broad-based recovery strengthens TXN's growth outlook beyond AI alone. Its manufacturing strategy, including 300mm wafer production, also supports long-term cost efficiency.
Texas Instruments generates substantial cash to fund investments and shareholder returns. Operating cash flow reached $9.9 billion over the trailing 12 months, while free cash flow totaled $8.4 billion. The company returned $5.8 billion to shareholders during this period and announced a 7% dividend increase, extending its streak of annual dividend increases to 23 years.
Nevertheless, TXN faces challenges. Its fourth-quarter 2026 revenue guidance of $5.8 billion to $6.3 billion suggests that sequential growth could moderate. Industrial and automotive demand can fluctuate with economic conditions, while manufacturing investments require substantial capital.
MU vs. TXN: Which Stock Has a Better Growth Profile?
Analysts’ projections suggest Micron has a better growth profile than Texas Instruments. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MU’s fiscal 2027 revenues and EPS indicates a year-over-year increase of 108.4% and 135.3%, respectively. For fiscal 2028, the consensus marks for revenues and EPS suggest year-over-year growth of 22.4% and 19.2%, respectively.
Meanwhile, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Texas Instruments’ 2026 revenues and EPS indicates a year-over-year increase of 23.4% and 55.8%, respectively. For 2027, the consensus marks for revenues and EPS suggest year-over-year growth of 12.5% and 18.3%, respectively.
MU vs. TXN: Which Stock Has the Better Valuation?
Micron has a clear valuation advantage, trading at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of just 4.69 compared with Texas Instruments' 28.76. This substantial gap makes MU appear significantly cheaper relative to earnings.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
The share price performance also favors Micron. MU has soared 200.1% year to date (YTD), substantially outperforming TXN's 61.1% gain. Although both stocks have benefited from rising semiconductor demand, Micron's stronger earnings momentum and AI-related opportunities demonstrate its superior performance.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
Texas Instruments deserves a premium for its diversified end markets, cash generation and consistent dividend growth. However, investors buying TXN at 29.3X earnings are paying considerably more for its established business model. articles.title: Solidigm confirms plans to build a fab in the US, abandons IPO plans — unfavorable stock market conditions and semiconductor share price trends reasons given - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Solidigm confirms plans to build a fab in the US, abandons IPO plans — unfavorable stock market conditions and semiconductor share price trends reasons given  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
SK hynix early on Friday announced that it had decided to abandon plans for a potential initial public offering (IPO) of Solidigm, its U.S.-based enterprise SSD subsidiary, citing unfavorable stock market conditions and semiconductor share price trends. At the same time, SK hynix confirmed it plans to build a new fab for Solidigm in the U.S. to address growing demand for enterprise SSDs. Although an IPO could have helped finance a new fab in the U.S., SK hynix claims that its subsidiary’s expansion remains a priority.
Solidigm specializes in high-capacity data center SSDs based on floating gate 3D QLC NAND memory. As AI infrastructure deployments accelerate, demand for high-capacity storage increases, whereas Solidigm's existing manufacturing capacity is barely sufficient to address its projected needs. Consequently, SK hynix believes that Solidigm requires additional production facilities in the U.S., although it has yet to disclose the planned fab's capacity, investment requirements, or construction schedule. Such a facility could also strengthen SK hynix's American manufacturing footprint, which is important, given the current environment and on-shoring trends.
SK hynix had considered multiple options — including direct investment, a pre-IPO funding round, and IPO of Solidigm — to finance capacity expansion. An IPO would have enabled SK hynix to raise capital from outside investors without taking on more debt. Furthermore, it could have revealed the true value of the subsidiary, which SK hynix believes is not properly reflected in its own market capitalization. In addition to financing the expansion, the proceeds could have been used for dividends, share repurchases, and share cancellations.
However, SK hynix says that increased market volatility and the ongoing correction in semiconductor stocks have made an IPO less attractive. As a result, the company believes that current market conditions would prevent Solidigm from achieving a valuation that adequately reflects its growth prospects. Consequently, it has discontinued its review of both pre-IPO financing and an IPO, even though it will continue to evaluate alternative funding mechanisms.
The cancellation of the IPO raises an obvious question: why would SK hynix abandon a financing mechanism that could provide billions of dollars for Solidigm's expansion just as demand for enterprise SSDs is at a record high and set to increase further over the next couple of years? After all, constructing a modern 3D NAND fab requires tens of billions of dollars, and external financing could reduce the burden on SK hynix's balance sheet and preserve capital for other projects (e.g., new capacity elsewhere).
One possible explanation is Solidigm's exceptionally strong profitability. Micron's enterprise storage division recently reported a non-GAAP gross margin of 90%, and given Solidigm's unique position in the market (it controls 21.1% of the enterprise SSD market together with its parent company), its margins may well be higher as it sells exclusive products. If extraordinary margins are sustainable over the next two or three years, its operations could substantially boost SK hynix’s consolidated profitability and generate considerable cash for future investments. Given these circumstances, SK hynix could potentially finance Solidigm's U.S. manufacturing expansion through a combination of internally generated cash and debt even without diluting its ownership. Financing the entire project with cash alone may also be possible, even though such an approach would be less likely given the massive capital requirements of advanced semiconductor production facilities nowadays. In any case, it is natural for SK hynix to prefer retaining full ownership of a highly profitable subsidiary to selling part of it at a valuation it considers inadequate.

articles.title: TSMC seeks rare-earth-free motors to reduce risk from China restrictions - Taiwan News
articles.summary: TSMC seeks rare-earth-free motors to reduce risk from China restrictions  Taiwan News
articles.full_text:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC is exploring factory motors that do not require rare-earth magnets to reduce supply risks from China's export restrictions, Reuters reported Thursday.
The chipmaker has asked suppliers about motors that can operate without rare-earth magnets in its automated factories. Three industry executives familiar with the discussions said the company was considering alternatives, but no large-scale changes have been made yet.
Rare earths are metals used to make powerful magnets found in many industrial machines. These magnets are used in motors that power automated equipment, including machinery found in semiconductor factories, per the International Energy Agency.
TSMC relies on automated equipment to produce advanced semiconductors. A shortage of specialized motors or replacement parts could disrupt chip production for customers in the smartphone, artificial intelligence, data center, and defense industries.
In 2025, China introduced export controls on certain rare-earth materials and related technologies. The restrictions require government approval for affected exports and have raised concerns about higher costs and supply disruptions for manufacturers.
Taiwan could face indirect supply disruptions because many rare-earth materials reach manufacturers through the US, Europe, and Japan. Hsu Tsun-tzu (徐遵慈), a researcher at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, said China's export restrictions could raise costs and create uncertainty for the country's businesses, per CTEE.
Taiwan and the US have also stepped up cooperation to secure alternative supplies of critical minerals. The two sides endorsed a US-led initiative in January to strengthen supply chains for advanced technologies, including semiconductors and artificial intelligence.
Taipei is developing its own rare-earth processing technology to reduce dependence on imports. Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said that the government planned to establish a pilot production line within three years that could meet about half of domestic demand, per CNA.
The country is also working on technology to recover rare earths from industrial and electronic waste. A government-backed research institute said it plans to begin transferring recycling technology to private companies this year, focusing on producing high-purity materials for industrial use.
The government is looking overseas for additional rare-earth supplies. Officials visited mining sites in Australia in May and planned an eight-day trip to the US in late October to meet mining companies and government officials.
Taiwan has also identified Canada as a potential source of rare-earth materials. The economics ministry aims to meet 50% of domestic rare-earth demand through local supply and processing by 2030.
Finding alternative sources remains difficult because China dominates the global rare-earth industry. The International Energy Agency said China accounted for 91% of global refined production of rare earths used in magnets and 94% of powerful permanent magnet production in 2024.

articles.title: Security Firm Discovers 32 NVIDIA B300 GPUs Operating Inside China Telecom, Showing U.S. Export Controls Aren’t Curbing Top-Tier AI Hardware From Getting Out - Wccftech
articles.summary: Security Firm Discovers 32 NVIDIA B300 GPUs Operating Inside China Telecom, Showing U.S. Export Controls Aren’t Curbing Top-Tier AI Hardware From Getting Out  Wccftech
articles.full_text:
NVIDIA’s flagship Blackwell Ultra B300 has continued to find a place in Chinese infrastructure after an investigation by security firm Lava revealed that 32 of these high-performance units were operating inside the network of China Telecom, a state-owned telecommunications giant. The report concludes that, despite the U.S. export controls in place, these GPUs are still finding a way onto Chinese soil, albeit through illegal means. Still, when there’s a trade ban in place, smuggling is the only alternative available to obtain NVIDIA’s latest AI hardware.
The restricted GPUs were remotely located, but NVIDIA doesn’t appear to be concerned, stating that it’s “a drop in the bucket”
Due to U.S. export controls, Chinese technology giants like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have been relying on GPUs like RTX PRO 5500 for AI inference, but it’s obvious that these graphics chips are inferior to the likes of the B300. However, what’s interesting is how China Telecom got a hold of NVIDIA’s Blackwell Ultra range, with The Information reporting that Israeli security firm Lava identified the restricted processors remotely via NVIDIA’s Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) Exporter tool.
Data center operators install this software for internal server health diagnostics, but the tool was accessible over the open internet without password protection. Though the software confirmed the existence of 32 B300 units operating on China Telecom’s network, their exact physical location couldn’t be determined. There’s no question why the trade ban is imposed on hardware like the B300 because with its 288GB of HBM3E memory across eight 12-high stacks, plus a memory bandwidth of 8TB/s on an 8,192-bit interface, it’s the most powerful AI acceleration architecture.
Able to handle demanding tasks like reasoning-based large language models, the B300 offers up to 50 percent higher memory and FP4 compute capabilities compared to previous generations. These performance gains and other attributes are exactly why the chip is subject to tight distribution restrictions. Under U.S. export policies, vendors can only sell B300 GPUs to whitelisted customers who commit to preventing diverted sales to embargoed parties. As you can see, despite trade barriers, illicit networks continue to move cutting-edge hardware into Chinese data centers, but NVIDIA doesn’t appear to be too bothered.
A company spokesperson told Tom’s Hardware that smuggled NVIDIA GPUs are “a drop in the bucket” compared to what China already possesses. In fact, the graphics chip manufacturer stated that diverted U.S. products make up less than 0.5 percent of deployed inventory. Still, if these 32 units were found inside China Telecom, who’s to say that more B300s won’t be found in other state-backed institutions?

articles.title: Intel CTO: EUV Tool Shortage Caps AI Chip Supply Growth at Roughly Double - Tech Times
articles.summary: Intel CTO: EUV Tool Shortage Caps AI Chip Supply Growth at Roughly Double  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Pushkar Ranade, Intel's chief technology officer, went on the record this week to explain why every billion-dollar fab announcement in the AI era ultimately collides with the same wall: the world produces fewer than 70 of the machines that make advanced chips, and that number will not change fast enough to matter for AI's current buildout timeline. Ranade made the remarks in an Intel fab tour podcast published Wednesday on the Dwarkesh Podcast, in a conversation that took Dwarkesh Patel through two days of tours at Intel's most advanced Oregon fabrication facility.
Speaking on the Dwarkesh Podcast in a conversation published Wednesday, Ranade said that when asked whether the semiconductor industry could expand advanced wafer output by a factor of ten to meet AI's escalating compute requirements, his answer was unambiguous: no. A doubling is closer to what the industry can realistically achieve, and even that would require a coordination effort across dozens of highly specialized suppliers that has never before been attempted at this pace.
That framing recenters the AI compute debate in a way few executives have been willing to do on the record. The conventional narrative focuses on which company will build the next fab — how quickly TSMC, Samsung, or Intel can pour concrete in Arizona or Ohio. Ranade's argument is that the constraint is upstream of every fab on earth: it lives inside the toolmakers' factories in Veldhoven, in the materials chains that feed cleanrooms, and in the specialist workforce that takes years to train. Capital alone cannot fix it.
What Limits the Industry Has Never Built Faster Than
At the center of Ranade's argument sits ASML, the Dutch company that manufactures every extreme ultraviolet lithography machine used to print the world's most advanced chips. EUV machines use 13.5-nanometer-wavelength light from a laser-pulsed tin plasma, operate in full vacuum with reflective optics instead of lenses, and weigh nearly 200 tons apiece. Only Zeiss in Germany can manufacture the multilayer mirrors at the optical precision these machines require, and only Oxford Instruments provides the synchrotron light source components. ASML does not make chips; it makes the machine that makes the machines that make the chips.
The 2025 global delivery total: 44 standard EUV systems. ASML confirmed for 2026 a target of roughly 65 Low-NA EUV shipments — up from 44 in 2025, a roughly 50 percent increase year-over-year. ASML's 2027 guidance calls for at least 80 units. These numbers set the hard outer boundary for how much additional advanced wafer capacity can physically come online.
ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet has said the pressure is real and structural. In a Reuters interview, he said demand for AI is so strong that the market will face constrained supply for quite a long time.
Each new EUV system arrives with an approximately 18-month lead time from order to delivery — meaning today's order backlog determines the hard ceiling on 2027 advanced-node wafer starts, regardless of urgency or premium pricing. Once delivered, reaching competitive manufacturing yields above 80 percent requires an additional 18 to 24 months of systematic process optimization. That is the compounding lag between a fab announcement and productive chip output.
Why the Constraint Gets Worse, Not Better, With Each Node Shrink
Here is what makes Ranade's ceiling structurally self-tightening in a way that is not immediately obvious: advanced chips require multiple EUV exposures per layer, and the number of exposures increases with each generation of node shrink.
The underlying physics is the cause. EUV produces stochastic defects — random pattern failures caused by the limited number of photons striking the resist at any given moment — at a rate that grows exponentially as features shrink. Managing this requires either higher dose (which slows throughput) or double and triple patterning (which multiplies the number of EUV machine-hours consumed per finished wafer). The result is that as AI accelerators push to tighter nodes, each chip demands more time on an EUV machine, not the same amount. The effective ceiling on wafer-equivalent AI chip output from the existing EUV fleet is not holding constant — it is declining relative to what the most advanced AI chips require.
This is the deeper layer of Ranade's argument. The "2× ceiling" he describes applies to the global tool base as a whole. For the specific chips that power frontier AI accelerators — which live on the most advanced process nodes — the practical constraint is tighter still.
Have You Asked Why Building a New Fab Does Not Break This Ceiling?
The logical response to a capacity shortage is more fabs, and the world has committed to exactly that. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta are collectively on track to spend approximately $725 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, much of it targeting AI infrastructure. GPU and accelerator purchases typically represent 30 to 40 percent of datacenter capital spending, implying chip demand that vastly exceeds what the current ASML delivery schedule can satisfy.
Building a fab does not help if the tools to fill it are backlogged. A leading-edge fabrication facility without EUV machines is a building. The machines arrive on ASML's schedule, are installed over months, are calibrated over additional months, and yield usable chips only after the process optimization cycle completes. This is why Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in the company's April 2026 earnings call that "advanced wafer capacity is in short supply" and that global semiconductor supply is not keeping pace with the rapid acceleration in demand — even as Intel was simultaneously ramping one of the world's largest advanced-node fabs.
An independent analysis of ASML's Q1 2026 results noted that even with 44 EUV units as the 2025 base, 80 units in 2027 implies EUV wafer capacity roughly doubling relative to 2025 — which is consistent with Ranade's framing and confirms the 2× ceiling from an external source. The arithmetic does not reach 10×.
Beyond Lithography: The Cascade of Constraints
The cascade does not stop at lithography. Even if ASML could triple its EUV output overnight, the semiconductor ecosystem would immediately collide with the next constraint: cleanroom capacity, process gases, ultra-pure water systems, photomasks, advanced packaging tools, and the trained workforce to operate all of them. Industry data shows that leading-edge logic, DRAM, and advanced packaging are operating at effectively 100 percent utilization, constrained not only by tools but by physical cleanroom floor space. High-bandwidth memory — the stacked chip architecture that feeds AI accelerators — consumes roughly three to four times the wafer area of standard DRAM per unit of memory delivered, compounding pressure on an already stretched wafer supply.
Intel's Specific Position Inside the Constraint
Ranade's comments are notable in part because Intel occupies an unusual vantage point: it is simultaneously one of the world's most ambitious advanced-node fabs and one of the industry's most significant customers of the tools he is describing.
Ranade holds a PhD in engineering from the University of California, Berkeley, and spent more than 17 years across two tenures at Intel working on transistor process integration — developing the manufacturing techniques for Intel's 65-nanometer, 45-nanometer, and 22-nanometer process nodes before being named chief technology officer in 2024. He also serves as Chief of Staff to Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan, placing him at the intersection of Intel's engineering roadmap and its commercial strategy. His assessment of the EUV ceiling is not theoretical — it reflects direct operational knowledge of how long it takes to ramp a leading-edge fab after the machines arrive.
Intel's High Numerical Aperture EUV commitment illustrates his point about cost and scarcity simultaneously. The EXE:5200B High-NA EUV machine, which Intel installed in late 2025 for its 14A process node, costs upward of $380 million per system — making it among the most expensive single pieces of manufacturing equipment ever built. Intel and ASML announced in September 2026 that Intel had processed more than one million wafers on High-NA EUV tools to date — more than the rest of the industry combined. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet, in an official joint press release, described Intel Foundry as "one of the key leaders of the industry's adoption of High NA."
Intel also broke ground in July 2026 on a Santa Clara campus expansion specifically designed to produce EUV photomasks for its 18A-P and 14A process nodes. Its Fab 52 in Chandler, Arizona, is designed to support more than 10,000 Intel 18A wafer starts per week at full ramp. Intel has confirmed that volume production on Intel 14A is targeted for the 2028 timeframe.
Every pound of concrete Intel pours in Arizona or Ohio, and every dollar it invests in High-NA EUV, still does not change how quickly ASML can build the machines themselves.
What Policy Can and Cannot Fix
The CHIPS Act and its equivalents in Europe, Japan, and South Korea can fund buildings, equipment deposits, and workforce training. What they cannot do is compress the multi-year sub-supplier ecosystem development that ASML's own production rate depends on. ASML works with approximately 200 main suppliers and roughly 2,000 companies in its broader supply chain. Expanding any link in that chain takes years of engineering qualification, capital investment, and production ramp — at every sub-tier simultaneously.
One geopolitical dimension is worth noting. Reuters reported in December 2025 that China had secretly completed a prototype EUV machine in Shenzhen, expected to produce working chips between 2028 and 2030. If accurate, this would eventually introduce a second manufacturer to a market ASML currently holds as a monopoly — but "eventually" is doing significant work in that sentence. Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.
The cost of EV batteries is spiraling downwards while the cost of gas and diesel is spiraling up. That’s a picture perfect scenario for accelerating the transition to EVs. The missing link is a level of battery performance that can meet, if not beat, a comparable internal combustion engine, and the Finnish innovator Donut Lab has just taken a -30 degree Celsius step in that direction.
One EV Battery To Rule Them All, Eventually
If the name Donut Lab rings a bell, run right out and buy yourself a cigar. CleanTechnica is among the many (many, many) EV enthusiasts following the Donut Lab story, which is a rather unusual one.
The company unveiled its new solid-state EV battery at the Consumer Electronics Show in January, describing it as “the world’s first solid-state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing,” while also pledging to share the results of third-party testing.
“With a full charge in five minutes and 400 Wh/kg of energy density, it seemed too good to be true. However, for any skeptics out there, Donut Lab is posting a new video series along with supporting material that explains the results of an independent assessment at the VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland,” CleanTechnica reported in January.
That’s right, VTT has been validating Donut Labs’s claims every step of the way, and the startup has been sharing those reports, in excruciating detail. In a bit of clap-back at skeptics who are challenging its claims, Donut Lab directs the curious to the VTT reports on its website at I Donut Believe.
New EV Battery Takes The Heat…
Donut Labs has kept VTT hopping since the big unveil. In March, VTT issued a report that validated the new battery’s performance at 100°C — in other words, the boiling point. That led some Donut-watchers, including CleanTechnica’s Christopher Arcus, to conclude that the battery is not based on lithium, as some others have surmised.
“Speculation that the Donut Lab battery is not real are diminishing as independent lab data shows 100° Celsius performance. Speculation that the battery may be lithium run[s] into difficulty explaining how a battery can work at 100° Celsius,” Arcus observed.
“In the independent tests, the thin membrane surrounding the pouch breached. If the contents were a standard lithium-ion with liquid electrolyte, there would have been significant outgassing and the organic electrolyte would have caught fire,” he further noted.
…And Cracks The Cold Code
In the latest news, earlier this week Donut Lab posted a new VTT report validating that the new battery retains 99% capacity at temperatures down to -30 degrees Celsius (-22 degrees Fahrenheit), a claim the company made at the CES unveiling. The cold weather validation is meaningful because it pulls the rug out from under EV critics, who are fond of claiming that cold weather significantly limits battery performance and range.
Cold weather can impact EV battery range, but then again, cold weather also puts a crimp on the fuel efficiency of gas-powered engines, too. Whether gas or electric, most drivers are in the habit of planning trips to make sure they don’t get stranded by the side of the road in cold weather or, for that matter, any weather, which lets a little steam out of the anti-EV argument.
Still, there is always room for improvement. EVs can be engineered with thermal management systems that protect against performance loss in extreme temperatures, but Donut Lab makes the case for doing away with external systems and building resilience into the battery itself.
The VTT test regimen involved a module consisting of 14 battery cells, placed in a temperature chamber at -30°C and left there for five hours. After the module was completely frozen through, tests showed that it retained 97% of its ampere-hour capacity, compared to a previous measurement at +25°C (about +77°F).
“As the report demonstrates, following battery capacity discharges performed during deep-freeze conditions, the module charges and discharges completely normally, with no adverse effects whatsoever resulting from the cold,” Donut Labs summarized in a press statement. The company further emphasized that the testing process did not include any heating, cooling, or insulation systems.
“We intentionally eliminated all the potential advantages a battery might normally have,” Donut Lab CTO Ville Piippo elaborated. “Despite this, the battery remained unaffected by the conditions. A typical lithium-ion battery would struggle to provide power, even for a brief moment, in such cold temperatures.”
Piippo also emphasized that the new battery eschews add-ons for temperature control. “This validates our promise of 99% capacity, which customers can expect from a fully insulated battery module without any heaters or tricks,” Piipp added for good measure.
Want more? Check out the YouTube video or download the VTT report.
EV Battery Mystery Solved…Not!
Because Donut Labs is taking everyone on a step-by-step validation journey, there are still some steps left to climb before a whole-of-system report is conclusive. And, the big mystery wrapped around an enigma remains: what, exactly, is in this new battery?
That’s a good question. One likely candidate is — or was — the NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) formula, but that idea has sunk like a lead balloon.
Meanwhile, over here in the US both Ford and General Motors have teased that the Next Big Thing in EV batteries is the LMR (lithium manganese-rich formula). The idea is to compete with lower-costing LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) batteries on cost, while out-performing LFP on energy density.
Last month, GM let word slip that its existing EV battery factory in Spring Hill, Tennessee, will begin producing LMR batteries for the electric mobility market.
Ford has been somewhat less forthcoming on the LMR topic of late, which is understandable because the company’s long-awaited Fathom electric pickup truck is poised for volume production next year. At a relatively affordable price point of just under $30,000 the truck will probably showcase LFP batteries.
At least, that was the case last year. “To really deliver truly affordable electric vehicles to our customers, we made a decision years ago to fully invest in a new facility with world-class LFP production technology installed in the U.S. for the first time — wholly owned and operated by Ford,”explained the company’s VP of Technology Platform Programs and EV Systems in an explainer posted in June of 2025.

GM has virtually tested more than 300,000 EV battery designs before building a single physical cell, according to Fortune. Specifically, the company used 300 million computing hours, which equals about 34,000 years on one computer. As a result, GM went from its first battery pack concept to formal approval in just one month.
Notably, the simulations focus on a new battery type called lithium manganese-rich, or LMR. According to GM, this chemistry holds 33% more energy than lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries at a similar cost. In addition, it uses 30% to 40% nickel, compared to about 85% in today’s high-nickel cells. However, LMR has long struggled with short battery life, and GM claims it has now solved that problem.
Furthermore, these simulations support GM’s upcoming fourth-generation EV platform. According to the company, the new platform will deliver about 20% more range per kilowatt-hour than current GM vehicles. On top of that, its electric motors will have 40% fewer parts than current models. The platform also uses 30% less wiring and includes a central computer with 40 times more processing power.
“High-nickel batteries will continue to give customers the highest range in our portfolio, while adding LMR positions us to leapfrog today’s more affordable chemistries and deliver lower costs with better performance,” said GM in a press release.
Additionally, GM says the approach will cut its usual four-to-five-year development cycle in half. For example, air flow simulations that once took 60 hours now finish in just 60 seconds. Meanwhile, GM’s factory system called PlantBrAIn already moves battery packs through assembly 30% faster. The company also uses virtual models to test assembly steps and equipment layouts before building real factory lines.
GM and LG Energy Solution will make the LMR cells at their Ultium Cells factory in Spring Hill, Tennessee. In addition, GM’s $900 million battery plant in Warren, Michigan, will reach full operation later this year. The company then expects volume production to begin in 2028. GM’s VP of battery Kurt Kelty also said, “We’re not licensing this from China.”
GM first shared these plans at its GM Forward event in New York this week. In fact, the company says it will invest more than $16 billion in US research and manufacturing this year alone. Overall, GM believes AI-driven development will help it compete with Chinese automakers on both speed and cost.

articles.summary: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising  Ars TechnicaGoogle makes a privacy policy exception to use your Gmail and Photos data for ads  Android AuthorityNow Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads  The VergeGoogle will target ads based on Gmail, Photos data if Personal Intelligence is enabled  9to5GoogleGoogle Privacy Policy: Gmail Ads Opt-In, Oct. 16 [2026]  shattered.io
articles.full_text:
Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.
On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.
This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.
Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.
According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:
“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”
Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

Three AI companies spent a combined $7.5 million on federal lobbying in the third quarter of 2026, each reaching its highest quarterly total on record, according to an analysis of newly filed disclosures by POGO. That figure represents a 22% increase from the previous quarter and roughly 60% more than the same period a year earlier.
The issues driving that spending are not abstract. Federal rules currently taking shape could affect AI safety requirements, chip export restrictions, copyright liability, and who pays for the electricity your local AI data centers consumes.
The Numbers Behind the Records
Each company reached a milestone it had never previously hit in a single quarter.
Nvidia led the quarter at approximately $2.2 million, the first time the company exceeded $2 million in a single quarter. Anthropic followed at about $2.1 million, roughly double its highest quarterly total from 2025. OpenAI reported about $1.5 million, according to The Verge's analysis of the disclosures.
OpenAI's growth trajectory is particularly notable. The company did not exceed $500,000 in a single quarter until late 2024 and did not clear $1 million until 2026, reflecting a rapid expansion of its Washington presence over a short period.
What Each Company Reported Lobbying On
Disclosed agendas span export controls, child safety, copyright, and the question of who foots the bill for data-center power.
Nvidia's reported lobbying covered 6G networks, responsible AI design, competition policy, quantum computing, and export controls. Export-control policy could affect the company's ability to sell advanced chips to overseas customers.
Anthropic reported lobbying on AI provisions in the child safety Kids Online Safety Act and export controls under the AI Overwatch Act. Its agenda also included an executive order concerning the naming of advanced AI or superintelligence, and the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill that would shift electricity costs from ratepayers toward data-center developers.
OpenAI's reported contacts ranged across Congress, the White House, the Commerce and State departments, and the Small Business Administration. Its disclosed topics included copyright, cybersecurity evaluations for frontier AI models, AI safety oversight frameworks, and antitrust protections for information sharing among competitors.
Still Playing Catch-Up With Big Tech
Established technology companies continue to outspend the newer AI firms, though the gap is narrowing.
Context matters here. Microsoft has reported at least $2 million in quarterly lobbying spending since 2021, according to The Verge, while Google regularly exceeds $3 million per quarter. Apple set its own record this quarter at $3.1 million, covering intellectual property, tariffs, child-safety rules, competition policy, and domestic semiconductor manufacturing.

articles.title: Starlink saga shows why Europe must catch up in space - Financial Times
articles.summary: Starlink saga shows why Europe must catch up in space  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Two stark events, barely a week apart, ought to focus minds in Brussels on the need to bolster European presence in space. First a throttling of Elon Musk-owned Starlink’s satellite network hampered Ukraine’s air defences and its own drone strike campaign. Then Andrew Puzder, US ambassador to the EU, warned of “devastating” retaliation if the bloc proceeds with plans to favour European companies when spectrum suited for satellite-to-device internet communication comes up for renewal.
Both incidents show how Europe’s reliance on US technology leaves it vulnerable in commercial and security terms. Under President Donald Trump, pressuring Brussels to protect US companies from regulatory constraints has become policy. But Washington risks undermining its own commercial interests. Threats and technological restrictions only reinforce European fears that the US is willing to weaponise their dependence. Ironically, Puzder’s intervention strengthens the case for the bloc to rapidly build up its own capabilities in critical technologies.
Recognising the need for autonomy, however, is easier than achieving it. Nowhere is that clearer than in low Earth orbit, where satellites operate close enough to the ground to provide reliable, high-speed internet connectivity. Musk’s SpaceX was early to see the demand, and adept at raising the vast resources needed to scale up its rocket-launching operations and drive down costs. The company has transformed the economics of space. Last year, SpaceX conducted 170 launches, compared with just eight by European providers. Europe lags behind in satellite networks, launch capacity and cost competitiveness. That leaves it — and Ukraine — dependent on American technology for the foreseeable future.
Europe could close some of the gap by harnessing the scale of its own market, which it has so far failed to do. Giving European companies greater certainty of demand — much as Brussels is pursuing a “Buy European” approach in other strategic sectors — would encourage investment and help drive down costs. Indeed, combined with the security imperative, there is a strong case for reserving some satellite spectrum for European operators. On Monday, four of Europe’s largest telecoms groups announced plans for a joint spectrum bid.
But preferential access to the European market alone is not enough. Europe also needs to quickly scale up satellite manufacturing, foster competition among launch providers and co-ordinate procurement to give companies confidence to invest. Even then, matching established rivals on price will take time, requiring carefully targeted public funding.
There are signs of progress. The EU’s IRIS² programme aims to develop a sovereign satellite communications network, while the bloc’s new arctic strategy identifies spaceports and launch services as priorities. The EU’s space programmes and the separate European Space Agency, of which the UK is part, have also seen their funding boosted. What matters is turning these initiatives into a competitive industry, rather than a collection of national projects and protected incumbents.
Being the first mover in an innovative technology that requires massive scale is how many US and Chinese industries came to dominate markets ranging from satellites to digital services. Europe cannot hope to replicate every part of America’s space industry, nor should it seek to shut out foreign competitors. But in technologies essential to its security and economic resilience, it needs credible alternatives. The Starlink saga should inject fresh urgency into Europe’s efforts to develop them.

Saudi Arabia's Humain has expanded its partnership with US chip maker Nvidia to develop up to 84 megawatts of artificial intelligence computing capacity, including infrastructure for an unnamed American customer, as the kingdom accelerates its push to become a global AI hub.
The agreement, announced at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin on Thursday, covers about 27,000 advanced graphics processing units (GPUs), with deployments beginning later this year and further capacity planned for 2027.
The expansion builds on a partnership announced in May 2025 during US President Donald Trump's visit to Riyadh, when Nvidia unveiled plans to supply Humain with hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips over five years. The initial phase involved 18,000 Blackwell processors, part of a broader plan to develop up to 500MW of AI computing capacity over five years.
The first phase of the latest agreement will comprise 14MW of Nvidia's Blackwell HGX B300 systems, equivalent to about 6,000 GPUs, with deployment starting in the fourth quarter. The infrastructure will support Humain Cloud customers, including AI companies, government entities and businesses.
A further 70MW of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin infrastructure, representing about 21,000 GPUs, is planned from mid-2027.
Of that, 50MW will be dedicated to advanced AI workloads for an unidentified US client, with deployment targeted to begin in June. The remaining 20MW will support Humain Cloud, with deployment expected to begin in July or August.
The companies said the Vera Rubin projects remain subject to final agreements and deployment plans.
GPUs are powerful processors used to train and run AI systems. Blackwell is Nvidia's current generation of AI chips, while Vera Rubin is its successor, designed to handle more complex workloads faster and more efficiently.
“We are moving quickly to bring the next generations of Nvidia-accelerated computing into Saudi Arabia at meaningful scale,” Humain chief executive Tareq Amin said.
Launched in May 2025 and chaired by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Humain is owned by the kingdom's Public Investment Fund and plans to develop about 3GW of data centre capacity by 2030 and more than 6GW by 2034.
Saudi Arabia is competing with the UAE to attract AI investment. In Abu Dhabi, G42, OpenAI and Oracle are developing Stargate UAE, a 1GW computing cluster that forms the first phase of a planned 5GW UAE-US AI campus, with Nvidia also a technology partner.
Both Gulf countries depend on US export approvals to obtain advanced AI chips, making Washington's technology restrictions an important factor in their expansion plans.
The latest announcement comes days after Saudi Arabia postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference from October 26-29 to next year. This followed a Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10 that killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300.
Mr Amin was among the speakers scheduled to attend gathering, which has become a major platform for announcing investment agreements involving Saudi Arabia's technology and infrastructure sectors.
The FII Institute says the annual conference has helped to secure $250 billion in signed agreements and investment pledges since its inception.

articles.title: NVIDIA B300 China Telecom: 32 GPUs Spotted [2026] - shattered.io
