articles.full_text:
An Israeli security firm called Lava says it spotted 32 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs tied to China Telecom, a state-owned carrier. Wccftech, TelecomTV, TechRadar and news.lavx.hu all carried the story between October 22 and 23, 2026. The finding landed in a year when every new Nvidia export headline gets read as a verdict on Washington’s chip policy.
The details matter more than the headline. Lava identified the chips remotely, through NVIDIA’s DCGM Exporter monitoring tool, and it could not pin down where the hardware physically sits. None of the coverage shows that China Telecom bought, owns or houses the GPUs. None explains how the chips got onto the associated network. This analysis separates what the reports establish from what readers are tempted to infer.
The story also sits next to other China-and-Nvidia items we have tracked, including a reported $35B Nvidia GPU order that tested export limits. Taken together, they show how much attention now follows every sighting of top-tier AI silicon near Chinese networks. Below, we walk through the facts, the export-control rules, the market stakes and what comes next.
What Lava Reported About 32 NVIDIA B300 GPUs
Lava, an Israeli security company, reported identifying 32 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 chips associated with China Telecom. Some outlets shorten the product name to NVIDIA B300, but the full name is Blackwell Ultra B300. The count of 32 is the headline number across the coverage, and no report we reviewed offers a different figure.
The reported discovery date runs October 22 to 23, 2026, depending on the outlet. That one-day spread is a reporting difference, not a conflict over the facts. Wccftech, TelecomTV, TechRadar and news.lavx.hu each framed the story around the same core claim: a security firm saw flagship Nvidia hardware connected to a Chinese state-owned telecom operator.
China Telecom is a state-owned telecommunications company, which is why the association drew fast attention. A carrier of that profile sits close to government priorities, and AI compute is one of them. Still, an association on a network is a narrow observation. It tells you that a monitoring signal tied the GPUs to that network. It does not tell you who ordered them, who pays for them or who can touch them.
Lava did not publish, in any report we reviewed, a chain of custody or a named seller. The coverage also lacks a verified on-record quote from a named speaker about this specific discovery. So we paraphrase the outlets here and attribute every claim to them. Where the sources go quiet, we say so rather than fill the gap.
How DCGM Exporter Exposed the Chips
Lava found the GPUs remotely through NVIDIA DCGM Exporter, according to the coverage. DCGM Exporter is a data-center GPU monitoring tool. Operators generally deploy it so that dashboards and alerting systems can read the health and workload of their accelerators. It exists to help administrators, not to track hardware across borders.
That origin makes the finding interesting. A monitoring component can reveal that specific GPU models are running behind a given network, even when nobody intended to broadcast it. The reports do not spell out which metrics Lava read or how the exporter became reachable. We will not guess at the mechanics. What the outlets do agree on is the method: remote observation of DCGM Exporter, not a raid, a leak or a customs record.
Why remote telemetry only goes so far
Remote observation can establish that a device is there and what it is. It rarely establishes where a rack stands. Network associations follow routing, hosting and tunnels, and those can span countries. Lava itself said it could not determine the exact physical location, and that caveat appears in the reports from the outlets above.
Think of it like seeing a phone number with a foreign dialing code. You learn something about the line, and you learn nothing certain about the handset in someone’s pocket. The same logic applies to a GPU reporting through a given network. The signal points at an association, and every conclusion beyond that needs further evidence.
What the Reports Confirm and What They Do Not
Readers will meet a lot of confident summaries of this story. Many skip the limits of the evidence. The table below sorts each claim by whether the available reports support it. We built it from the verified facts across the Wccftech, TelecomTV, TechRadar and news.lavx.hu coverage.
| Claim | Status in the reports | What the coverage says | 
|---|---|---|
| Lava identified 32 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs | Confirmed | Reported across all four outlets | 
| The GPUs are associated with China Telecom | Confirmed (association only) | A network link, not proof of ownership | 
| Lava used NVIDIA DCGM Exporter to find them | Confirmed | Remote identification | 
| Discovery date October 22 to 23, 2026 | Confirmed | Date varies by outlet | 
| Exact physical location known | Not established | Lava could not determine it | 
| China Telecom purchased, owns or houses the GPUs | Not established | No report makes this case | 
| The GPUs were smuggled into China | Unconfirmed | No evidence of route or intent | 
| The find proves export controls are failing | Unconfirmed | An inference, not a finding | 
| Price, shipment date, seller or buyer | Unconfirmed | None disclosed | 
The bottom half of that table is where most social posts go wrong. A GPU tied to a Chinese carrier’s network can mean several things, and only a few of them involve a rule being broken. We return to those possibilities below.
Why the NVIDIA B300 Matters: 288 GB HBM3E and 8 TB/s
The Blackwell Ultra B300 is a top-tier data-center accelerator. Reports list its memory at 288 GB of HBM3E with 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. Those two numbers explain the interest. Large language model training and serving often hit memory limits before they hit raw compute limits, so a chip with that much high-bandwidth memory sits near the top of any buyer’s wish list.
| Item | Reported detail | 
|---|---|
| Product name | NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 (shortened to NVIDIA B300 in some coverage) | 
| Memory | 288 GB HBM3E | 
| Memory bandwidth | 8 TB/s | 
| Units reported near China Telecom | 32 | 
| Export status | Subject to U.S. export controls | 
| Who may buy | Approved (whitelisted) customers who agree not to transfer chips to sanctioned parties, including China | 
| Detection method | NVIDIA DCGM Exporter, observed remotely | 
Thirty-two GPUs is a small number by hyperscale standards. A single large training cluster can use many times that count. So the sighting does not, on its own, signal a frontier-scale training run. What it signals is access. If even a few top-tier parts show up behind a sensitive network, policymakers and competitors will ask how many more exist that nobody has measured.
We stop short of any performance claim about what 32 B300s could do for a specific workload. The sources give memory and bandwidth only, and we will not extrapolate beyond them. Readers who want to compare the part with other accelerators should wait for official spec sheets rather than leaked or inferred figures.
The Export-Control Rules Around B300 Sales
According to the reports, B300 GPUs fall under U.S. export controls. Nvidia may sell them only to approved customers, the whitelisted group. Those buyers agree not to pass the chips to sanctioned parties, and China is named among them. The structure is simple on paper: approved buyer in, no onward transfer out.
The simplicity ends once the hardware ships. After delivery, enforcement depends on contracts, audits and the honesty of resellers. A system integrator might host chips for several customers. A cloud provider might lease them out. Each step adds a party who can, deliberately or not, move capacity somewhere it should not go. The rules cover the buyer’s promise. They cannot physically follow a rack.
That gap is why monitoring-based discoveries like Lava’s attract attention. They offer an outside view of where approved hardware ends up. They also expose the limits of that view. Without the exact location, the seller or the chain of custody, regulators cannot tell whether the observation points to a violation, a permitted arrangement or a misread network trace.
Nothing in the coverage says U.S. authorities have opened a case over these 32 chips. We found no named official speaking about the matter on the record. Any statement about enforcement action would be speculation, so we leave it out.
Five Ways 32 B300s Could Appear on a China Telecom Network
The reports leave the explanation open. The table below is our own analysis, not a finding from Lava or any outlet. It lists plausible readings of a network association and what each would require. Treat it as a map of questions, not a set of answers.
| Scenario | What it would mean | What would support it | 
|---|---|---|
| Hosted outside China | Approved hardware sits in a facility abroad and connects through a China Telecom link | A confirmed data center address outside China | 
| Leased or shared capacity | An approved owner rents access, so the network sees the GPUs without owning them | Lease terms or a hosting contract | 
| Test or demo hardware | A short-term lab setup, possibly cleared in advance | A vendor or partner disclosure | 
| Hardware inside China | Chips physically sit in China, which would raise export-control questions | A verified physical location and an import trail | 
| Misattributed network data | The association comes from routing or labeling, not a true link | Independent checks that contradict the trace | 
Only one of those five rows involves chips physically inside China, and the reports do not confirm it. That is the hinge of the whole debate. If later evidence shows a Chinese location and an unauthorized transfer, the story changes sharply. If it shows a hosted or leased setup abroad, the story shrinks to a curiosity about network telemetry.

articles.title: Finland to Help Build Satellite Communications that Ukraine Controls - Eyes Only with Wes O'Donnell
articles.summary: Finland to Help Build Satellite Communications that Ukraine Controls  Eyes Only with Wes O'Donnell
articles.full_text:
Ukraine just signed an agreement with Finland to explore something that sounded fairly boring a month ago, and suddenly got extremely important:
Satellite communications that Ukraine actually controls.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo oversaw the signing of seven agreements in Kyiv yesterday (October 22) covering defense production, drones, transportation, construction, and space. The agreements have a combined estimated value of around €300 million.
The document that caught my attention was signed by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, Nokia Defense, and ICEYE.
According to Zelenskyy, the three parties signed a letter of intent aimed specifically at developing Ukraine’s satellite communications capabilities. Zelenskyy said Kyiv had agreed to make “greater use of Finland’s satellite capabilities” for both defense and national resilience.
I think that wording undersells what Nokia and ICEYE are proposing.
They’re really talking about helping Ukraine develop sovereign satellite communications.
The wake-up call came when Musk throttled Ukraine’s Starshield service, and as of October 23, 2026, Ukraine says the restrictions remain in place.
(Even though Musk says service has been restored.)
I’ve spent a lot of ink this past week writing about who possessed the contractual authority to change those settings, but the larger lesson keeps bothering me more.
Ukraine built an enormous portion of its battlefield communications architecture around a satellite network it didn’t control; because it trusted the supplier.
And Starlink has been extraordinary technology for Ukraine. It survived Russian electronic warfare, attacks against terrestrial infrastructure and the general abuse of operating in the world’s nastiest electromagnetic environment. Ukrainian soldiers have wired the system into command posts, vehicles, boats and increasingly drones.
Then, infuriatingly, Musk changed a software permission.
That is the vulnerability Nokia and ICEYE say their new system is intended to remove.
And interestingly, they started building it before the Starlink mess.
In an incredible bit of foresight, Nokia and ICEYE announced their sovereign satellite communications partnership on October 1, nearly two weeks before Ukraine began experiencing the SpaceX restrictions.
Their proposal is a broadband low-Earth-orbit communications system intended specifically for governments, defense organizations, border agencies, and emergency services.
The first communications satellites are expected to launch in 2028.
So, Ukraine hasn’t suddenly panic-ordered a Finnish replacement for Starlink. The project was already moving. The Starlink episode just demonstrated the requirement in the most spectacular way possible.
ICEYE says the goal is to provide Ukraine with secure satellite communications “that it controls.” Nokia says the same basic thing from the networking side: governments need communications that remain available under pressure while national authorities retain control over the connectivity their military depends on.
That gets us to the technical question of today’s piece...
What does sovereign satellite communications actually mean? Well, your country has to own the important bits.
Ukraine already knows ICEYE extremely well.
In August 2022, the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation purchased access to ICEYE’s synthetic aperture radar constellation and transferred the capability to the Ukrainian government. The deal gave Ukraine full use of one ICEYE satellite already in orbit along with access to imagery from the broader constellation.
That satellite became known in Ukraine as the “People’s Satellite.” Kind of like The Rock Dwayne Johnson used to be the “People’s Champion” in wrestling before he became a movie star.
Ukraine’s military intelligence said within months of getting access, ICEYE imagery had helped identify thousands of pieces of Russian military equipment, including tanks, artillery, helicopters, air-defense systems, and Iskander positions.
Then the relationship kept growing.
In January 2026, ICEYE announced another agreement expanding Ukrainian access to high-resolution SAR imagery for tactical military decision-making. So Ukraine already understands what it means to integrate Finnish commercial space technology into military operations.
But the new project changes the mission. ICEYE has historically looked down.
Now, with Nokia, it wants to help governments talk through space too.
Nokia brings the nervous system
If ICEYE provides the spacecraft and space experience, Nokia brings much of the communications architecture connecting everything together.
That means secure networking, network orchestration, ground infrastructure, and terminals; the whole shebang.
The two companies say their planned system will integrate satellites, ground stations, and ruggedized end-user terminals into one sovereign architecture.
ICEYE says its approach gives governments ownership and operational control over the satellites, ground segment, and terminals. Its own description of the service goes even further: customer data can remain entirely inside approved national or allied infrastructure, without dependence on a foreign commercial operator’s terms of service.
That’s a nice little middle finger to Elon.
So, I think there are three ways Ukraine could do this…
One is a dedicated national constellation.
Ukraine owns the satellite system and operates it for Ukraine. That’s the purest form of sovereignty and probably the most expensive.
A second option is a coalition constellation shared among allied countries. That possibility gets really interesting. Imagine Ukraine, Finland, Poland, the Baltic states, and perhaps several other European countries collectively operating a low-Earth-orbit military communications constellation.
Each contributes funding and infrastructure and the network provides overlapping coverage. Control remains within the coalition rather than residing with a foreign commercial provider.
The third option is what ICEYE calls a “hosted sovereign service.”
That would presumably allow a government to gain protected capacity more quickly without immediately funding an entire constellation from scratch, while still preserving much tighter national control over data and service than a conventional commercial subscription.
We don’t yet know which model Ukraine is considering, the October 22 document is just a letter of intent.
Plus, the first Nokia-ICEYE communications satellites aren’t expected to launch until 2028 and Ukraine still needs Starlink today.
I have to admit that I didn’t fully appreciate the vision when I first learned about Starlink. But remember, back then, Ukrainian-style drone war hadn’t been invented yet. My biggest concern was the sky pollution hampering astronomers’ observations.
But now the benefit is obvious… Starlink’s enormous advantage is scale.
SpaceX operates more than 11,000 satellites across Starlink’s constellation, giving it coverage and capacity that no competitor can immediately reproduce.
Ukraine has thousands upon thousands of terminals already distributed across its military and civil infrastructure.
Its soldiers know how to use them.
Its units have built tactics around them.
Replacement terminals exist.
Commanders know roughly what the network will tolerate.
A new Finnish satellite system isn’t going to magically replace all of that in 2027, nor are Nokia and ICEYE claiming it will. Their own literature says the sovereign constellation is intended to complement commercial and governmental networks rather than replace every other system.
That’s probably how Ukraine should approach it…
Military communications shouldn’t have one backbone, but several.
Starlink can be one. ICEYE-Nokia can become another. Europe’s IRIS² and GOVSATCOM infrastructure can eventually add additional paths. Terrestrial fiber and microwave links remain important. Military radio still works in a pinch, when Ivan’s not jamming shit.
Different systems overlap so that losing one doesn’t suddenly blind an entire battle group.
That’s just redundancy, (like we had on the AWACS):
There were two complete radar chains starting with two different high power amplifiers (Klystron Power Amplifiers or KPAs) all the way up to the antenna element in the rotodome. It was up to the on-board radar tech which chain, A or B, you’d be flying that day; but if one went down, you could switch to the other chain with no mission interruption. (When both chains went down on the same flight, the mission fails… but you get to go home early.)
Plus, there’s a second story happening underneath all of this.
Finland and Ukraine are developing a strange defense relationship, and I mean that in the best possible way.
In the same package of agreements, Ukrainian and Finnish companies agreed to explore joint production of unmanned military systems inside Finland. Patria is involved. Ukrainian drone companies are involved. Zelenskyy says measures worth around €200 million are already underway under the broader Ukraine-Finland Drone Deal.
Then there are the locomotives.
Finland agreed to give Ukraine ten Dv12 diesel locomotives and spare parts free of charge, becoming the first country to donate locomotives directly to Ukrzaliznytsia.
Ukraine says Russia has damaged or destroyed nearly 600 locomotives since the full-scale invasion, including more than 300 diesel units.
I’m deliberately not going down that rabbit hole here because I think Finnish locomotives quietly joining Ukraine’s war deserve their own video. I’ll be filming this for next week’s YouTube slate.
Anyways, taken together, these agreements show Finland doing something increasingly common among Ukraine’s northern European partners: integrating Ukrainian wartime experience into Finnish industry while giving Ukraine access to capabilities Finland happens to be very good at building.

Cobalt market participants at the recent Antaike Nickel and Cobalt Forum (13–15 October) and LME Week (19–23 October) events in China and London respectively have uniformly reported weak pricing sentiment. This is driven by soft LCO demand and large stocks of cobalt sulphate, precursor cathode active material (pCAM) and recycled material in China. Huayou, Greatpower, Tengyuan and CTT have halted metal production, while Greatpower’s salt line is running at only 20% utilisation.
Several sources told Benchmark they expect the DRC to cut export quotas by 25% next year, with some traders anticipating an announcement in late October or early November, whilst others are expecting intervention in January or February 2027.
“A 25% quota cut would land on a market that is already well supplied with intermediates, so the price response will depend on how quickly Chinese stocks are drawn down,” said George Ingall, senior analyst at Benchmark.
Black mass emerges as key feedstock
Chinese sulphate producers increasingly rely on recycled material, and several sources told Benchmark the cheapest sulphate in the market comes from black mass, with most estimates of recycled cobalt supply sitting between 30kt–45kt per year.
During Antaike’s Forum, European cobalt metal prices sat at $21–23/lb, which was well above the $16–17/lb heard in China. During LME Week, the European market corrected down, with transactions heard in the range of $17.5-19.5/lb. Market participants also tempered hopes that Indonesia can fill any DRC shortfall, with expectations voiced of Indonesian MHP output of 40–50kt rather than the 60–70kt expected in China.
Dislocation raises demand for transparent reference prices
“With prices this fragmented, reliable reference points matter more than ever,” Ingall said.

articles.title: ‘The West can’t stop me’: Space wars heat up as Russia tails a Ukraine-linked US satellite - Defense News
articles.summary: ‘The West can’t stop me’: Space wars heat up as Russia tails a Ukraine-linked US satellite  Defense News
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Washington blamed Moscow at the United Nations on Wednesday for deliberately moving a Russian military satellite with an undisclosed mission “dangerously” close last week to a U.S.-registered satellite believed to serve Ukraine, with officials vowing to defend American interests in space.
The Russian satellite, Cosmos 2612, spent more than two weeks maneuvering toward ICEYE-X36, a radar satellite operated by the American arm of Finnish company ICEYE that supplies imagery to Ukraine’s military through some of its spacecraft, then shadowed it from as close as a third of a mile through the weekend of Oct. 17.
U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas G. DiNanno called the Russian satellite’s behavior “threatening,” and said the country had been “intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.”
Space historian and former NASA astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell said that he believed it is the first rendezvous in low Earth orbit between two active satellites without one owner’s approval.
The close encounter came weeks after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink publicly confirmed that the U.S. has weapons in orbit and the Space Force picked two companies to build space-to-space reconnaissance satellites. It also followed reports that trillionaire Elon Musk — under White House orders — slowed the military-grade Starlink that Ukraine relies on, rendering some of the country’s essential air defense weapons useless.
The operation fits a wider Russian campaign of intimidation against Europe and the U.S. that lets Russian President Vladimir Putin “poke the West in the eye and watch the West do nothing,” according to Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“They prove a point – the West can’t stop me,” Swope added Wednesday during a CSIS panel on the encounter.
As the U.S. and its allies increasingly rely on commercial capabilities for national security, key assets like satellites have “become vulnerabilities that can be exploited by our adversary,” according to Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Virginia-based Integrity ISR, who also spoke on the CSIS panel.
The impact of a possible satellite attack could reach well beyond one company or country, since commercial satellites now carry much of the imagery and connectivity militaries fight with, experts said. Musk’s Starlink slowdown in Ukraine showed how quickly a military force can suffer when that access is throttled without notice — and how easily local geopolitical conflicts can explode into global security crises.
On Oct. 12, commercial trackers feeding the U.S. military’s Joint Commercial Operations cell flagged the possible rendezvous when Cosmos 2612 slid into ICEYE-X36’s orbit roughly 345 miles above Earth, according to Integrity ISR’s newsletter.
On Oct. 15 and 16, the Russian satellite moved from more than 200 miles behind ICEYE-X36 to roughly 3 miles away before moving in closer and holding position through the weekend, tracking firm LeoLabs said in a statement reported by CNN.
Both satellites travel at roughly 4 miles (7 kilometers) per second, so getting two objects “within a hundred meters or even a kilometer” of each other is “the equivalent of flying in a very tight formation in an aircraft,” Gillinger said.
“Russia didn’t accidentally get within a kilometer of X36,” he said. “It is an indication of intent that they’re sending a message.”
ICEYE, whose radar satellites see through clouds, smoke and darkness, expanded cooperation with Ukraine’s military, pledging continued imagery “on tactical timelines,” according to a January statement. However, the company has not confirmed which of its satellites serve Kyiv.
Moscow has warned since the first year of its full-scale invasion that Western commercial satellites helping Ukraine could become legitimate military targets.
ICEYE said it is “aware of the situation and tracking it closely” and that its “constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine earlier this week.
Russia’s intent behind the satellite maneuvers remains unclear. According to LeoLabs, an American space technology company, possible aims range from intelligence collection and close inspection to coercion and groundwork for future operations against satellites.
The maneuvers demonstrated capabilities that could be used to “inspect, characterize, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft,” though they “do not establish hostile intent,” the company said.
Analysts could not yet say whether Moscow planned an attack and then reversed course, or was orbiting nearby for another purpose entirely.
Russia could have been doing “a dry run” for a future attack, or the satellite could have been carrying a weapon, from a jammer to a laser to a projectile, Swope explained.
“Was the intent to blow up the satellite? No,” he said. “Was the intent to put some type of energy on the satellite? Probably… I don’t know why you’d need to maneuver in this way, this close, unless you wanted to do something that involved putting energy on that satellite.”
The Russian satellite has since pulled back, but not far.
It was again flying at ICEYE-X36’s altitude on Wednesday, holding roughly 250 miles (400 kilometers) behind it, and could “easily close that gap again at the time and place of their choosing,” Gillinger said.
Russia could try to approach another ICEYE satellite within weeks, as two more satellites from the same launch will soon line up with the orbit of a second satellite, ICEYE-X37, according to Integrity ISR.
If they move in, “we could see another scenario where another commercial satellite is closely trailed by one of these Russian satellites,” Gillinger said.
The retreat began Oct. 18, two days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving tariffs and most economic restrictions on Russia.
Swope said Trump’s move to ease sanctions “could have been a reason why Putin said, ‘You know, now’s not the time to exacerbate tensions specifically with the United States. Maybe we should pause this operation.’”
“If you’re getting close to a deal on something, why jeopardize that?” he said.
The potential for a conflict in space has been growing in recent months.
Washington “appears to lack response options” if Russia threatened U.S. military and commercial satellites with a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to the conclusions from a 2025 war-game scenario where fictional Russian space objects threatened American interests.
There is no public indication that Cosmos 2612 carries a nuclear weapon, but Swope said that there is also still no internationally recognized rule for determining if a maneuver like this one should be considered hostile — or what international standards should be followed in a response.
“Even though we all can make a good case on why this was [hostile], there’s no norm that you could point to,” he said.
Without a clear response plan or real consequences for aggression, menacing satellite moves like this one are “literally just a spigot that Russia could turn on and off” to increase pressure on adversaries, Swope said.
Russia, he added, “is going to turn it on again.”

articles.title: Explainer-What is going on with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine? - The Lufkin Daily News
articles.summary: Explainer-What is going on with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine?  The Lufkin Daily News
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON/KYIV, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine's military has been hit this month by restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system. Its receivers stopped functioning when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones, jeopardising some combat and air defence missions.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that SpaceX boss Elon Musk had restored services, although he has denied having spoken to Musk personally about it. But Ukrainian defence and military sources told Reuters on Friday that speed restrictions on Starshield remained in place.
HOW DOES UKRAINE USE STARLINK AND STARSHIELD?
Ukraine's military uses both Starlink for communications and Starshield for specialised military purposes.
The satellite internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival with the capabilities of SpaceX's products.
Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. But the recent limitation cuts them off when moving faster than 160 kilometres per hour (100 mph).
Ukrainian officials say that hinders drones used for strikes on Russian targets deep inside Ukraine and in some high-speed interceptors to counter Russian drone attacks.
Ukraine's use of Starshield-enabled mid-range attack drones has been a major factor this year in turning the tide on the battlefield, allowing remote pilots to guide drones striking moving targets such as Russian supply trucks and trains.
And fast-moving interceptor drones are one of Ukraine's few systems to protect its cities from one of Russia's own major innovations of recent months: jet-engine-powered attack drones, now used in strikes each night.
WHO GAVE THE ORDER TO RESTRICT IT?
Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for curtailing Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, and both have said publicly such decisions could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters reported last week that the order to limit the system came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The Wall Street Journal, however, reported on Wednesday, citing sources, that the throttling had been ordered personally by Musk.
After the limitations became public, Musk said that Starshield was owned and controlled by the US government, and that any limits on its speed or usage were decided by the US military and ultimately by Trump. He contrasted this with the commercial Starlink system, which he said was not designed or authorised for military use.
Trump has denied being involved in any decision concerning the slowdown. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that âdecisions regarding Ukraine's access to âStarlink were up to SpaceX and Musk, not the White House.
The restriction comes amid a low point in relations between Kyiv and Washington as Trump seeks to push Kyiv into accepting stronger concessions in a peace deal with Moscow.
Trump has also been pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, although Starshield is not used on drones conducting those attacks as it does not operate over Russian territory.
HOW DOES STARLINK WORK?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
WHAT IS STARSHIELD?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink satellite constellation as their backbone.
In addition to secure communications, SpaceX says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using Starshield services costing five times as much.
(Reporting by Joey Roulette, Cassell Bryan-Low and Max HunderEditing by Joe Brock and Peter Graff)

articles.full_text:
Update, Fri 23 Oct, 11:10 ET: As reported by Reuters, the FCC announced on Thursday that it had decided to grant a waiver to Intel from a ban on the purchase of foreign-made robots. The original of the report remains below as first published.
Intel has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to make an exception for the automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that the company uses to transport the sensitive silicon wafers and other materials, containers, and supplies needed to make the most advanced chips in its fabs. According to Bloomberg, the American chipmaker fears that its AGVs would fall under the blanket prohibition against foreign-made robots after they were added to the FCC’s Covered List.
AGVs are niche machines that chip fabs use to transport materials and supplies between tools and sections of the fab, helping ensure that the cleanroom conditions required for each manufacturing process are maintained. This makes them critical equipment for U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, but, apparently, there are no suitable domestic alternatives for these devices at the moment. Intel’s current fleet of AGVs requires continuous maintenance, including software and firmware updates, and if it’s forced to find a local supplier for its AGVs, the company says that it would take years, crippling the United States’ chipmaking efforts.
The biggest AGV suppliers are Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., while a few smaller businesses from South Korea and Taiwan are also trying to break into the market. It’s unclear why these companies haven’t applied for a conditional approval yet, which would allow them to continue selling these products in the U.S. while also promising Washington that they’ll set up a manufacturing base in the country. This is something that Netgear has already done, allowing it to continue selling its foreign-made routers despite being an American company.
Intel says that it remains unclear if updates to its AGVs would break compliance with the FCC, and that it’s asking the agency to issue a conditional waiver “out of an abundance of caution to ensure the ongoing operation of these specific AGV units.” While Team Blue is the only company concerned about AGVs at the moment, other chip manufacturers would likely need a similar waiver in the near future, especially as they build more fabs in the U.S. This includes TSMC, which is planning to build 12 more fabs and four packaging facilities in Arizona, Samsung, with its new Taylor, Texas, fab, and even Elon Musk’s Terafab, which has already begun construction.
Washington has been using the FCC to force companies to invest in American manufacturing. Its blanket bans on foreign-made products like drones and routers have affected some of the biggest brands in the U.S., including DJI and TP-Link. While these bans do not outright ban the sale of all products made by these companies, especially those that have already been approved before, they make it impossible for them to introduce new products and even release software updates to their existing product line. The FCC eventually walked back on the software update ban, but they still would not be able to register new products unless they build them in the U.S.

A policy change hasn't been announced, which is why China's response could very well be considered an overreaction. A Franco-German proposal would enable Britain's participation, but with a catch. That catch is to align with EU trade defense measures. The legislation remains under negotiation as of this writing. The alignment condition would pull British trade policy much closer to Brussels than London might otherwise choose.
As a case in point, the EU imposed additional countervailing duties of up to 35.3 percent on Chinese battery-electric vehicles. Add the standard 10 percent levy to that, and you get a maximum combined rate of 45.3 percent. If Britain were to follow suit, Chinese automakers would be greatly hindered by said tariffs.
Speaking of alignment, the European Commission plans an annual cap of 350,000 Chinese hybrid vehicles from December 2026, reducing China's share of the EU hybrid passenger vehicle market from 6 to 3 percent. Britain's participation would also hurt China, hence the ministry's rather aggressive reaction.
As it stands, China wants the UK to understand that trade restrictions come with consequences outside the automotive industry. While it has not named potential targets, China doesn't appear to be bluffing here. As for the UK, post-Brexit woes could very well be the catalyst for playing ball with the EU.

General Motors (GM) has revolutionized electric vehicle (EV) battery development by virtually testing over 300,000 battery configurations before producing any physical cells. This extensive simulation approach, utilizing approximately 300 million computing hours—equivalent to roughly 34,000 years on a single computer—enabled GM to finalize a battery pack design in just one month.
Advancing Battery Technology with LMR Chemistry
The simulations primarily focused on a novel battery chemistry known as lithium manganese-rich (LMR). GM claims that LMR batteries offer 33% greater energy density than conventional lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries while maintaining comparable costs. Additionally, LMR cells incorporate 30-40% nickel, a significant reduction from the typical 85% nickel content in current high-nickel batteries.
Despite previous challenges with battery longevity associated with LMR chemistry, GM states it has addressed these issues, supporting the rollout of its upcoming fourth-generation EV platform. This platform is expected to deliver around 20% more driving range per kilowatt-hour than existing GM vehicles, alongside streamlined electric motors featuring 40% fewer parts, a 30% reduction in wiring, and a central computer with 40 times increased processing capacity.
Implications for U.S. EV Industry and Manufacturing
GM’s innovative simulation methods are also shortening the traditional development cycle—the company anticipates reducing what typically takes four to five years by half. For instance, air flow simulations that used to require 60 hours can now be completed in just a minute, while the assembly process in their PlantBrAIn factory has accelerated battery pack production by 30%. These virtual models even assist in optimizing factory layouts before construction.
The LMR battery cells will be manufactured at the Ultium Cells plant in Spring Hill, Tennessee, a joint venture between GM and LG Energy Solution. Meanwhile, GM’s $900 million battery facility in Warren, Michigan, is slated to reach full operational status later this year, with mass production expected to commence in 2028.
GM Vice President of battery technology Kurt Kelty emphasized the company’s commitment to domestic innovation, stating, “We’re not licensing this from China.” With an investment exceeding $16 billion in U.S. research and manufacturing this year, GM aims to leverage artificial intelligence and advanced simulation to remain competitive internationally—particularly against Chinese automakers—by accelerating timelines and lowering costs.
Why This Matters for Pakistan
GM’s pioneering use of AI-driven battery design and manufacturing signals a transformative shift in automotive innovation that is reshaping the global EV landscape. For Pakistan, a nation keen on expanding its electric vehicle market and manufacturing base, GM’s advances highlight the importance of integrating digital technologies and investing in local research capabilities to compete globally.
As the electric vehicle industry grows rapidly worldwide, Pakistan’s stakeholders can draw lessons from GM’s model to enhance local production efficiencies, develop cost-effective battery technologies, and reduce dependence on imported automotive components. Incorporating such innovations could accelerate Pakistan’s ambition to improve green mobility, reduce fossil fuel reliance, and foster economic growth through technology-driven manufacturing sectors.

articles.title: Guest Post: Quantum Computing’s Next Phase May Be Driven by Compounding Breakthroughs - The Quantum Insider
articles.summary: Guest Post: Quantum Computing’s Next Phase May Be Driven by Compounding Breakthroughs  The Quantum Insider

Guest Post by Liam Wang COO, Logical Qubit Technology.
The World Economic Forum’s Quantum Economy Day 2026 was held in Geneva, Switzerland, on October 13–14. Logical Qubit Technology attended as the only quantum computing company representing China. The company’s Chief Operating Officer, Liam Wang, joined business executives, researchers, and representatives of international organizations from around the world to discuss the global development of quantum computing.
This June, I took part in a World Economic Forum discussion on global quantum science and technology development at the Summer Davos meeting in Dalian. Representing the company again at Quantum Economy Day 2026 in Geneva gave me a close-up view of how quantum computing is developing in other countries and regions.
What Is Everyone Talking About?
My first and most immediate impression: China and other countries share many of the same concerns about this industry — how to persuade policymakers, capital, and industry to commit more resources to quantum computing; which application scenarios will see the first breakthroughs; how geopolitics continues to shape the global industry (supply chain security, the setting of global quantum standards, and so on); how to broaden quantum computing’s social reach, steadily moving beyond academia into industry and the wider public; and how the convergence of quantum computing and AI will unfold, and what major opportunities that super-cycle will create.
Although the industry is still at an early stage, the overall mood among participants was optimistic. AI was the most common point of comparison: since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, the pace of progress in large AI models has exceeded almost everyone’s expectations. Quantum computing is likely to follow a similar logic.
Of course, at this stage, quantum computing still has to be viewed pragmatically. Two terms came up most frequently in the discussions: “use case” and “geopolitics.”
The first concerns what quantum computing can actually do. As at many conferences, its impact on classical cryptography was discussed first; PQC, QKD, and cybersecurity came up again and again. The consensus was clear: the world needs to prepare for Q-Day as soon as possible. Beyond that, drug discovery, chemical simulation, new energy and materials R&D, and financial applications were the most frequently cited use cases.
The geopolitics question is more complicated. Around the world, quantum computing depends on government policy support. Yet intensifying geopolitical competition is, to some extent, impeding global collaboration in the field — which helps explain why supply chain security was such a widespread concern in the room.
It is clear that the development of the global quantum computing industry — setting the technology itself aside — carries two overlapping spectra: competition among nations and competition among companies.
Competitive advantage will most likely come from:
(1) the capacity for action a country or company possesses, and the results it delivers — sustained policy support, for instance, or a company closing the loop on real-world applications faster.
(2) the depth of participation and voice in global competition and cooperation. Even though names like Google and IBM come up often, the quantum race has not consolidated into a handful of dominant players the way AI has. The more likely picture is one of regional competition between countries, interwoven with rivalry between companies.
Looking inward from these global gatherings: this year I had the honor of representing the company at VivaTech, Summer Davos, the Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong, and now Quantum Economy Day 2026. Beyond the chance to observe how other countries and regions are developing quantum computing, these events have prompted reflections on the industry at home, framed around three questions:
(1) How should we view the current stage of China’s quantum computing development?
(2) What new narratives might emerge in quantum computing?
(3) Where does China stand in the global quantum computing competition?
How Should We View the Current Stage of China’s Quantum Computing Development?
A caveat first: my perspective is not that of an academic or researcher, but a business-oriented one.
In the second half of 2026, the phrase I have heard most often is that quantum computing has “cooled off.” The evidence cited is mostly about investment and capital: valuations are too expensive; quantum stocks on U.S. markets have pulled back; and expected policy support for the domestic capital market has fallen short. Together, these factors have created the feeling that the industry has turned cold.
I believe that judging the industry by the “hot” and “cold” defined by investment and capital is too one-dimensional — it oversimplifies how quantum computing is actually developing. My description of this stage, and of the next three to five years in China, is “compounding breakthroughs”: over the long cycle toward universal quantum computing, the intervals between milestone events, large and small, are getting shorter, and the cumulative effect compounds — accelerating the arrival of the universal quantum computing era.
This judgment rests on five observations:
1.On technology: Google and the team of Academician Pan Jianwei at the University of Science and Technology of China have demonstrated quantum error correction below the error-correction threshold. China’s quantum companies are now anchoring their strategies on fault tolerance and investing heavily in error correction R&D. I expect that within one to two years, a commercial quantum computing company will reach an error-correction milestone.
2.On policy: at home and abroad, quantum computing has become a strategic priority in frontier technology. Intensifying competition between nations requires sustained policy support — support that in turn gives commercial companies the resources they need for technical breakthroughs and the validation of application scenarios.
3.On the ecosystem: 2026 can fairly be called year one of China’s quantum computing ecosystem. Alongside a new wave of hardware companies, software and algorithm developers and critical component suppliers are springing up like bamboo shoots. What deserves note — and what many overlook — is that collaboration across the value chain, between software and hardware, and between hardware vendors, is accelerating overall.
4.On industry: leading companies in pharmaceuticals, materials, finance, and AI are accelerating their engagement with quantum computing — not just through investment, but with sustained commitment at the business level. I believe that within one to two years, China will see flagship cases achieve verified commercial closed loops in limited scopes or specific domains.
5.Finally, on AI + Quantum: I share the consensus at Quantum Economy Day 2026 — AI + Quantum will become a super-cycle. Talk to entrepreneurs in China’s quantum sector and you will find that combining AI with quantum computing is a natural ambition. That expectation is strong at home and abroad alike.
What New Narratives Might Emerge?
This is also why I believe the industry’s development may have only just begun. Looking back at the wave of enthusiasm across late 2025 and the first half of 2026, it is easy to agree on one thing: policy support has been the core narrative fuel. It lifted the rocket off the ground — but reaching orbit will take more fuel. Which new narratives could supply it?
1. Fault-tolerant quantum computing results. Strictly speaking, this may not be a “new” narrative: expectations are remarkably aligned, at home and abroad, that the field’s next milestone is fault tolerance. The U.S. Department of Energy and companies including IBM, QuEra, and IonQ have published roadmaps targeting fault-tolerant quantum computing in 2028 or 2029. Chinese companies have not announced specific dates, but they are equally anchored to the goal.
Logical qubits are indispensable to fault tolerance. Recently, Matthias Troyer and Chetan Nayak of Microsoft’s quantum team, along with last year’s Nobel laureate in Physics John Martinis, emphasized the importance of scalable logical qubits. However it is defined, logical qubits — in meaningful numbers and quality — will become the next concrete milestone. When that happens, I believe enthusiasm in the primary investment market will reignite.
2.Deep convergence of AI and quantum computing. This expectation is equally strong. Over the past year, virtually every industry event has featured dedicated discussions of AI for Quantum and Quantum for AI. Many quantum companies are already applying AI across their R&D: AI agents helping optimize quantum circuits, dynamic circuit compilation to improve gate fidelity, and optimization of quantum error correction decoders. It is fair to say that the “AI penetration rate” of a quantum company’s R&D will become an important measure of its competitive edge. A team that uses AI to accelerate R&D and deliver breakthrough results will also hold an advantaged position in fundraising.
3.Sustainable business models. How quantum computing makes money has been the most challenging question of the past year. Any investor evaluating a quantum team will ask: what is this year’s revenue, and where will next year’s orders come from? Behind these questions lies a concern about whether the field can generate sustained income.
At present, orders for quantum companies at home and abroad come mainly from full-system delivery, so judging the industry by a hardware business model fits today’s reality. But high hardware prices, steep barriers to use, and heavy operating and maintenance costs make mass adoption difficult.

Finnish company ICEYE and Nokia have signed a letter of intent with Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore cooperation in the space sector. The parties will examine the possibility of developing a sovereign satellite communications network for Ukraine.
According to the announcement, the project involves secure broadband communications via low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. The system is intended to provide connectivity for defence purposes and critical government services, particularly when terrestrial infrastructure is compromised or disrupted.
The partners intend to build the system using European technology, ensuring state control over the satellite fleet, ground infrastructure, and user terminals. The companies view the network as a complement to existing military and commercial communications systems.
ICEYE CEO and co-founder Rafal Modrzewski stated that Ukraine requires secure, sovereign satellite communications under its own control. He also stressed that the company has supported Ukraine since 2022 and intends to continue doing so.
ICEYE already collaborates with Ukraine in space-based intelligence, providing imagery from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites. However, this new initiative focuses on a distinct domain: developing satellite communications infrastructure.
The parties have not disclosed the budget for the Ukrainian project, the number of satellites involved, or the deployment timeline. It also remains unclear whether the collaboration will entail establishing a dedicated satellite constellation for Ukraine.
In early October, ICEYE and Nokia announced a partnership to develop satellite communications networks for government clients. The first satellites under the joint initiative are scheduled for launch in 2028, though no specific timeline has been disclosed for the development or deployment of a system tailored for Ukraine.
Ukraine currently relies on Starlink satellite communications provided by US company SpaceX, alongside its military-grade variant, Starshield. In October, the provider introduced restrictions that sever drone connectivity at speeds exceeding 160 km/h.

articles.title: Iceberg Quantum Validates Pinnacle 1.2 Architecture with Crevasse QLDPC Decoder to Reduce RSA-2048 Factoring Resources - Quantum Computing Report
articles.summary: Iceberg Quantum Validates Pinnacle 1.2 Architecture with Crevasse QLDPC Decoder to Reduce RSA-2048 Factoring Resources  Quantum Computing Report
articles.full_text:
Fault-tolerant quantum architecture startup Iceberg Quantum has released Pinnacle 1.2, demonstrating direct circuit-level simulations of quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes that validate logical error rates below 10-12 per logical qubit-cycle—the threshold required to execute 2048-bit RSA integer factorization.
The breakthrough is enabled by Crevasse, Iceberg Quantum’s new QLDPC decoder. Crevasse achieves an average decoding latency of 4 microseconds per error-correction round, enabling the team to execute trillions of simulated error-correction cycles directly rather than relying on statistical extrapolations. By combining Crevasse’s decoding efficiency with compiled modular exponentiation circuits, Iceberg Quantum updated its resource estimates for breaking RSA-2048 to 72,000 physical qubits in 3.7 days at a physical error rate of p = 10-3 (and 48,000 physical qubits in 0.98 days at p = 10-4 for a 1-microsecond code cycle time), representing a significant reduction in spacetime overhead compared to Pinnacle 1.0.
| [ Pinnacle 1.2 RSA-2048 Factoring Resource Benchmarks ] |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Physical Error Rate (p) | Code Cycle Time (dt) | Physical Qubit Footprint | Expected Total Runtime | 
| • p = 10-4 | • 1 microsecond (Atomic / Photonic) | • 48,000 physical qubits (d = 10) | • 0.98 days | 
| • p = 10-3 | • 1 microsecond (Atomic / Photonic) | • 72,000 physical qubits (d = 16) | • 3.7 days | 
| • p = 10-4 | • 1 millisecond (Trapped Ion) | • 714,000 physical qubits (d = 10) | • 29 days | 
| • p = 10-3 | • 1 millisecond (Trapped Ion) | • 2.1 million physical qubits (d = 16) | • 32 days | 
| • Frozen Pinnacle (p = 10-3) | • 1 microsecond (Fixed-degree 8 Superconducting) | • 99,000 physical qubits | • 5.0 days | 
Direct Error-Correction Sampling and Circuit Compilation
To establish these metrics, Iceberg Quantum simulated one trillion samples across Pinnacle memory and processing blocks without encountering logical failures under smaller code distances: observing only three logical errors on its d = 16 ([[254,14,16]]) code at p = 10-3 (a logical error rate of 2 × 10-13) and zero logical errors on its d = 10 ([[126,12,10]]) code at p = 10-4 (≤ 3 × 10-13). The use of smaller code distances reduces spatial overhead by ~40% and temporal overhead by ~30% compared to Pinnacle 1.0 benchmarks.
The team verified complete modular exponentiation circuits against models of the Pinnacle architecture using forced-gap post-selection for state injection into magic state distillation blocks, achieving injection error rates of (1.3 ± 0.3) × 10-6 (d = 10) and producing output magic states with failure rates near pout ≈ 3.5 × 10-11. Applied to Frozen Pinnacle—a variant designed for fixed 8-degree connectivity superconducting systems—the improved compilation reduces resource requirements to 99,000 physical qubits and a 5.0-day execution runtime.

Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?



In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.



Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.



Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!



In the biotech world, you can’t see everything

articles.full_text:
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. 



I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.



Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.





In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.



Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.



Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.



Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.



In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.



It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.



As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?





I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?



But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.



I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?



One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.



Except that sometimes you can’t.



Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.



At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.



I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?



I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim. 



But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!



This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

articles.full_text:
Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
How tech billionaires are changing funding
With some big AI companies soon to go public on the stock market, the ranks of ultra-rich philanthropists in the United States look set to grow. Compared to government funding agencies, ultra-wealthy research investors tend to support projects that are higher risk and more personally relevant, with fewer strings attached. But there’s less oversight of philanthropic programmes, it’s difficult to assess their success and many are geared towards encouraging the use of the same technology the philanthropists profited from developing.
Image of the week
News
Global emissions slow — but not enough
Global greenhouse-gas emissions might have plateaued last year and there has been a faster-than-expected expansion of renewable energy capacity, finds the United Nations’ latest report on climate change. But without a major acceleration in emissions cuts, by mid-century average temperatures might hurtle past 2 °C — a ceiling that countries committed to in the Paris Agreement. The emissions slow-down is “definitely good news, but not good enough,” says climate scientist Bill Hare. Under current policies, scientists estimate warming to peak at 2.6 °C to 2.8 °C this century; there is also a smaller chance of warming exceeding 3.4 °C on the current trajectory, which would be catastrophic.
Reference: UN Environment Programme Emissions Gap Report 2026
Fossil records challenge extinction story
Palaeontologists have trained a machine-learning model on a huge database of fossil records, then used it to reconstruct a timeline of changes in Earth’s biodiversity over hundreds of millions of years in unprecedented detail. The model, called OneStrata, hints at several possible challenges to big ideas about evolutionary history. For example, it suggests that three of the “Big Five” mass-extinction events were gradual declines in biodiversity, rather than the sudden cataclysms described by other reconstructions.
Single antimatter particle caged for months
Physicists have suspended a single positron — the antimatter equivalent of an electron — near absolute zero and in a near-perfect vacuum, for months. Researchers hope to spot subtle differences between matter and antimatter that could shed light on one of physics’ greatest mysteries: why is there something rather than nothing.
Reference: Physical Review Letters paper
Body clock linked to 1 in 4 depression cases
A study of more than 11,000 people with depression found that a quarter had a new subtype that makes their condition hard to treat. ‘Circadian depression’ seems to be linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock, which could be targeted with treatments such as melatonin and light therapy. “Circadian depression is not just depression with bad sleep,” says neuroscientist and study co-author Emiliana Tonini. “There is an underlying biology that is quite distinct from other forms of depression.”
Reference: British Journal of Psychiatry paper
Can a human survive in a whale’s belly?
The ‘modern-day Jonah’ film Whalefall, based on Daniel Kraus’s 2023 novel, follows a university student who is accidentally swallowed by a sperm whale while scuba diving. Scientific advisor Joy Reidenberg, a comparative anatomist, and Ilias Foskolos, who researches deep-diving toothed whales, talk to Nature about glowing guts, stomach acids and why we probably don’t have to worry about any of this in real life.

Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

The Best iPad; The Worst Phone. John Gruber wrote a great review of the iPhone Duo, which we broke down on Dithering. In short, it’s an iPad that fits in your pocket, and it’s awesome at that; just don’t expect a good phone. Plus, on Monday we discussed Apple’s surprising partnership with Meta for edge AI, a topic I also covered in Tuesday’s Update. — Ben Thompson 









The SS Sarandos in a Storm. The past week has seen a flood of bad news for Netflix: layoffs, executive departures, another disappointing round of earnings, and another hit to a share price that has taken a 40% hit over the past 12 months. Wednesday’s Update provides a comprehensive state of the union, and we doubled back on the topic for a fun conversation on this week’s Sharp Tech, where we divided the company’s problems into areas that can be fixed (the content) and what may be much trickier (growing the business in a world where Meta and YouTube are primary engagement competition).— Andrew Sharp



You Can See Everything, But Can’t Trust Anyone. Allow me to be the 1,000th person on the internet to recommend Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything. After declaring on Sharp Tech last week that I wasn’t interested in seeing it, I did in fact check it out, and wound up loving it. I wrote about my experience on Sharp Text, with 5 spoiler-free notes for anyone still on the fence, and 5 more reactions for anyone who’s seen it. Compulsively watchable (and worth seeing in a theater), I think it may have also been the most effective document of our modern media environment I’ve ever seen. — AS









Presented by







It’s kind of weird to be the Internet’s number one fan of ads. What makes it even weirder is that I have been the Internet’s number one fan of ads without actually having ads on Stratechery. 



That second part is changing: I’m super excited to announce that Stripe is going to be the presenting sponsor of Stratechery. And, at the end of the day, for me it couldn’t be any other company.



One of my hangups in terms of advertising is that I take my ethics super seriously, and ultimately, if a company is helping pay the bills, it’s hard to be truly objective about them. What I realized, however, is that it’s hard for me to be objective about Stripe anyway. I wanted to be a professional blogger long before I started Stratechery; however, I thought I had missed my chance, particularly as it became clear that advertising was not a long term business model for a one-person site. However, when Stripe launched with support for recurring billing, I realized there was a better model: subscriptions. 13 years later, and I’m still a happy customer. Or, to put it another way, I’m already conflicted because I love Stripe. I’m not the only one: more than 5 million businesses use Stripe, accounting for 1.7% of global GDP. Moreover, a lot of those businesses are Internet native and accretive to the world’s economy, which is to say that Stripe is literally making the world a better place. That’s an easy company to get behind, especially since they have been behind Stratechery from the very beginning. — Ben Thompson

A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO."
The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.
Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read-and-write access to portions of system memory.Read full article

articles.summary: "We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders."
articles.full_text:
During a lengthy news conference on Friday, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis Program.
Although much of the information behind these plans has been previously reported at Ars Technica and elsewhere, this marked the first time NASA has laid them out in detail and acknowledged some substantial changes in the architecture.
Most notably, for SpaceX's Starship vehicle, the revised plan calls for the Orion spacecraft to dock with the Starship lunar lander in high-Earth orbit before transiting to the Moon. And for Blue Origin, the mission architecture includes four launches of the New Glenn rocket, but no spacecraft-to-spacecraft refuelings. articles.full_text:
Leaders in the US Space Force would like to have a new spaceport up and running in four years, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure from bases in Florida and California that have shot rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years.
The obvious problem with that ambition is 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink first mentioned the service's search for a third launch base in May. A congressionally mandated study of the Space Force's launch infrastructure identified the need for "another site that's capable of heavy and super heavy launch capability," Meink said in a House Armed Services Committee hearing.Read full article

articles.title: Spotify ramps up policy enforcement on family plans
articles.summary: If you share Spotify sub with family, you may need to scan QR code to prove it.
articles.full_text:
As reported by Music Business Worldwide, Spotify appears to be stepping up enforcement of existing policies regarding Family and Duo subscription plans by requiring users to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager's device in order to maintain access to it. Those who fail to scan the address verification QR code within seven days will see their account demoted to the free tier and be barred from joining any other Duo or Family plan for 12 months.

      Spotify's QR code plan enforcement.
        Credit:
          Spotify
      
Spotify's support documentation verifies the policy after users on Reddit began posting reports of receiving the QR prompt. The enforcement stems from Spotify's requirement that family plan members reside at the same address—a seemingly reasonable policy in concept. But what if you have a child away in college, a spouse who works on the road, or any number of other circumstances that might see families separated by physical distance? The policy could extend beyond friend groups looking to save a buck, affecting actual families who thought they were using the program as intended.
Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15 Music in the Air: 10 Years On report, made available by HITS Daily Double, estimate that "a meaningful share of family plan users are not actual household members, but rather friends sharing a plan to reduce costs." The report goes on to add, "We see additional monetization upside from tightening household verification on multi-user plans. Most family plans require members to reside at the same address, but enforcement has been minimal in practice."Read full article

articles.title: Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals
articles.summary: Birds' compact nervous system seems to help them handle tasks very quickly.
articles.full_text:
Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. In a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision.
But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions.
“This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?”Read full article
